Data Science as Scientific Practice
Week 1, Day 1

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Welcome!

Instructors: Dr. Gretchen LeBuhn & Dr. Nicole Adelstein
Today’s Focus: Thinking clearly about data
What to expect: - Get to know each other - Surface big ideas in data science - Establish course norms

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What This Course Is About

This is a course about thinking clearly with data.
Not about: - Being a coder already - Memorizing functions - Learning statistics in isolation
About: - Explaining your reasoning - Spotting your assumptions - Revising when things don’t make sense

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
You Belong Here

Prior coding experience is not what matters.
What matters: - Willingness to ask “why” - Explaining your choices - Revising when things are unclear
That’s science. We’re applying it to data work.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
How Today Will Work


Get to know each other through noticing patterns in data
Surface big data science ideas without code
Talk about norms for working together

I’m watching how you think, not what you already know.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Introductions as Data

Put three things in the chat:

Your name
Your field or program
One kind of data you work with (or hope to work with)

Not sure what counts as data? Just write what comes to mind.
Never worked with data? Write that.
All answers are useful.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
A Question

Did everyone interpret “data” the same way?
(Answer in chat or unmute)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Ambiguity in “Data”

Some people answered with: - Format (Excel, CSV files) - Content (genes, behavior, measurements) - Collection method (surveys, sensors)
The ambiguity doesn’t go away when you start coding.
It just gets buried under syntax.
The hardest part of data science? Deciding what you’re even measuring.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
This Class as a Dataset

Breakout Activity (10 minutes):
Imagine describing this class as a dataset for someone who wasn’t here.

What variables would you include?
How would you define them?
What information do you wish you had?

Write your reasoning, not just a list.
Google Doc link in chat →

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Did We Learn?

Three groups will share:
One interesting decision you made
OR
One place where you got stuck

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Example: Measuring “Experience”

“Experience” could mean: - Time in grad program - Prior statistics courses - Comfort with ambiguity - Years working with data
You didn’t fail because you couldn’t agree.
You succeeded because you noticed the decision you’d have to make.
That’s data science.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What We Just Did

Without writing a single line of code, you:

✓ Defined variables
✓ Noticed ambiguity
✓ Made decisions and justified them
✓ Realized others might make different decisions

This is the foundation of everything we’ll do this semester.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Course Norms

My commitments to you:

I will not assume you know things
I will not mistake speed for understanding
I will not treat “I don’t know” as failure
I will give you time to think

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What I Need From You


Ask questions out loud — if you’re confused, someone else is too
Try things when you’re not sure — messy reasoning > polished guessing
Be kind to each other and yourselves

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Your Turn

Two questions (chat or unmute):

What do you want to accomplish this semester?
What do you need from me or from each other to make that happen?

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What I’m Hearing


You want to feel competent, not just compliant
You want to understand, not just copy
You want space to struggle without judgment

We can work with that.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Before Wednesday

Think about this question:
What decisions did we make today that felt invisible at the time?
We’re not writing code yet, but we’re already making choices about what counts, what matters, and how to define things.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Final Thought

Everything we did today — thinking, struggling with definitions, noticing ambiguity —
That’s not “pre-data-science.”
That IS data science.
The coding is just execution.
The thinking is the work.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
See you Wednesday!
Come ready to learn about decision logs.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reproducibility & Decision Logs
Week 1, Day 2

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Welcome Back

Monday: We noticed how ambiguity shows up in simple questions
Today: How do we work with data in ways we can defend, reproduce, and share?

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Monday Was About

When you defined variables like “experience” or “field,” you were making data decisions:

What counts
What doesn’t count
How to measure fuzzy concepts

Those decisions get embedded in your work.
Today’s question: How do we make those decisions visible, defensible, and reproducible?

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Today’s Plan


What is reproducibility?
What is a decision log?
Practice writing one entry
Critique each other’s writing
Connect to project organization

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Sound Familiar?

You work in Excel…
Calculate something…
Copy to Word…
Make a figure…
Paste it…
Email yourself a version…
Save: Analysis_Final_v2_REAL_final.xlsx

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Then Your Advisor Emails

“Can you redo this with the updated data?”
And you think:
“…I have no idea what I did.”

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Is Reproducibility?

Someone else — or future you — can take your data and your process and arrive at the same results.
Not just the same numbers.
The same reasoning.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Three Types of Reproducibility

Computational: Your code runs the same way on different computers
Empirical: Your data collection is documented well enough to repeat
Conceptual: Your decisions are clear enough to understand why
Today’s focus: Conceptual reproducibility

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why This Matters

You’re always collaborating with future-you.
And past-you doesn’t respond to emails.


If you don’t write down why you made a decision: - You won’t remember it in two weeks - You can’t defend it - You can’t reproduce it

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Tool: The Data Decision Log

A running document where you write:

What you decided
Why you decided it
What else you considered
What trade-offs you made

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Example Decision Log Entry

Decision: Converted all “dawn” entries to 6:00 AM.
Reasoning: Dawn in our study area ranges from 5:45–6:15 AM. Using 6:00 introduces <30 minutes of error, acceptable given our 2-hour observation windows.
Alternative considered: Exclude “dawn” entries entirely. Rejected because it removes 18% of early-season observations.
Trade-off: Slight temporal imprecision in exchange for retaining sample size.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What This Entry Does


Transparent — not hiding reasoning
Shows alternatives — not just first idea
Acknowledges trade-offs — doesn’t pretend the decision was obvious

This is scientific thinking applied to data work.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Your Turn: Writing Practice

10 minutes of silent, independent writing
Use the same structure: - Decision - Reasoning - Alternative considered - Trade-off
Google Doc template in chat →

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Scenario

You’re analyzing bee diversity data from urban gardens. Your dataset has a “Garden Type” column with:

Community garden
Community Garden
community garden
Comm. garden
School garden
school garden (community-maintained)
Private yard
private yard (open to public)

Task: Write a decision log entry explaining how you would standardize these categories — and why.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Silent Writing Time

10 minutes
Start now.
(Optional: quiet music)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Peer Review

Breakout rooms of 3 (12 minutes):

Each person reads their entry aloud (1-2 min)
Others give feedback:

One thing that was clear
One place you wanted more explanation


Goal: Help each other see where clarity breaks down

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Made Writing Hard?

Not the specifics of your scenarios—
What made clarity hard?
What made writing difficult?
(Chat or unmute)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“How much detail should I include?”

Guideline:
Write enough that a colleague could understand your reasoning without asking follow-up questions.
If they’d need you there to explain it, you didn’t write enough.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“Is my reasoning good enough?”

There’s no “good enough” in the abstract.
There’s reasoning that’s defensible given your constraints and reasoning that’s not defensible.
Not defensible: “I combined them because they seemed similar”
Defensible: “I combined community and school gardens into ‘public gardens’ because both involve shared maintenance and open access, even though governance structures differ”

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“I hadn’t thought through alternatives”

That’s the value of writing it down.
Writing reveals what you haven’t thought about yet.
That’s not a bug — that’s a feature.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“It was hard to admit trade-offs”

We’re trained to present conclusions, not uncertainty.
But science IS trade-offs.
Pretending they don’t exist doesn’t make your work stronger—
It makes it fragile.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Core Pattern

Writing forces you to be explicit about things you thought you’d already decided.
That’s uncomfortable.
That’s essential.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
When Do You Use This?

Write in your decision log when:

Choosing between two reasonable options
Combining or recoding categories
Excluding data (ALWAYS)
Making an assumption that could be challenged
Something didn’t work (so future-you doesn’t repeat it)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Test

If someone asked in a meeting:
“Why did you do it that way?”
And your honest answer is:
“Um… I’m not sure”
→ You should have written it down.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
How This Connects to Structure

Decision logs record your reasoning.
But they only work if your files and workflow are also reproducible.
Organized project: - One folder per project (RProject) - Organized subfolders (raw data, processed data, scripts, figures) - Relative file paths (works on anyone’s computer)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Structure Matters

If I can’t find your data
and I can’t run your code,
your decision log is just a story.
It’s not reproducible.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What We’re Building Toward

A way of working where:

Your data stays raw (never overwrite originals)
Your process is scripted (no manual copy-paste)
Your decisions are documented
Your file paths are robust (work on any computer)

Everything connects.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Before Next Class

Low-stakes assignment:

Open R or RStudio
Just look at the interface
Open a blank script file
Type your name
Save it
Close it

That’s it.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Such a Simple Task?

Coding anxiety comes from learning the tool and the concepts at the same time.
Get comfortable with what RStudio looks like before we ask it to do anything.
Separate the fears. Tackle them one at a time.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Resources

In the chat:

Decision log template (use all semester)
R/RStudio installation troubleshooting guide

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Final Thought

Everything we did today — writing, peer review, struggling with clarity —
That’s not “pre-data-science.”
That IS data science.
The coding is just execution.
The thinking is the work.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
See you next time!
Come ready to look at R with curiosity, not fear.

10.1 Status Badge Guide

title: Data Decision Log
text:
10.2 When to Write an Entry
Write a decision log entry when:

You’re choosing between two reasonable options
You’re combining or recoding categories
You’re excluding data (ALWAYS document exclusions)
You’re making an assumption that could be challenged
Something didn’t work and you want to remember why
Someone might ask “why did you do it that way?”

Don’t document:

✗ Obvious or trivial decisions
✗ Standard procedures followed exactly as documented
✗ Exploratory poking around (unless you learn something important)

title: Data Decision Log
text:
10.3 The Quality Test
Could a colleague/classmate understand your reasoning without asking follow-up questions?

If YES → You wrote enough
If NO → Add more explanation


This decision log is version controlled with Git. Use commit messages like “Add decision about outlier handling” to track the evolution of your analytical thinking.
Remember: The thinking is the work. The code is just execution.

title: Week 1, Day 2: Reproducibility and Decision Logs
text:
Duration: 75 minutes | Online Synchronous | 30 students




Test platform
Prepare decision log template (Google Doc)
Load scenario slide
Prepare breakout rooms (groups of 3)
Queue quiet background music for silent writing time (optional)





[0:00–0:04] — Settling In
Good morning, and welcome back to day two!
On Monday, we did something that might have felt simple — we introduced ourselves, we talked about this class as if it were a dataset, and we noticed how quickly ambiguity shows up even in simple questions.
Today, we’re going to connect that experience to something bigger: how we actually work with data in ways that we can defend, reproduce, and share.
Take a breath. We’re going to move slowly and deliberately.

[0:04–0:08] — Naming What Monday Was About
Before we go forward, I want to name what we did on Monday.
When you defined variables like “experience” or “field,” you were making data decisions. You were deciding: - What counts - What doesn’t count
- How to measure something that’s actually quite fuzzy
Those decisions don’t disappear when you start coding. They get embedded in your work — sometimes invisibly.
Today’s question is: How do we make those decisions visible, defensible, and reproducible?




[0:08–0:10]
Here’s what we’re doing today:

I’ll introduce the idea of reproducibility — what it means, why it matters
We’ll talk about decision logs — a tool for writing down your reasoning as you work
You’ll practice writing one entry
We’ll critique each other’s writing to see where clarity breaks down
I’ll show you how this connects to how we organize our work

By the end of today, you’ll have a template you can use all semester.
Questions? Chat or unmute.




[0:10–0:15] — The Problem
Let me show you something.
[Show slide: messy Excel workflow — copy/paste chaos, files named “Final_v2_REAL_final.xlsx”]
Does this look familiar?
You work in Excel, you calculate something, you copy it into Word, you make a figure, you paste that too. Maybe you email a version to yourself. Maybe you save three copies with slightly different names.
Then your advisor says: “Can you redo this with the updated data?”
And you think: “…I have no idea what I did.”
[Pause for effect]
Sound familiar? You can admit it. We’ve all been there.

[0:15–0:19] — Defining Reproducibility
Reproducibility means: Someone else — or future you — can take your data and your process and arrive at the same results.
Not just the same numbers. The same reasoning.
There are different kinds of reproducibility:

Computational: Your code runs the same way on different computers
Empirical: Your data collection is documented well enough that someone could repeat it
Conceptual: Your decisions are clear enough that someone understands why you did what you did

We’re focusing on that last one today — conceptual reproducibility.

[0:19–0:22] — Why This Matters
Here’s the thing: You’re always collaborating with future-you.
And past-you doesn’t respond to emails.
If you don’t write down why you made a decision, you won’t remember it in two weeks. You definitely won’t remember it in two months. And if you can’t remember it, you can’t defend it.




[0:22–0:30] — Introducing the Log
So here’s a tool I want you to use: a data decision log.
It’s just a running document where you write down: - What you decided - Why you decided it - What else you considered - What trade-offs you made
Let me show you an example.
[Show slide with example entry]:
Decision: Converted all "dawn" entries to 6:00 AM.

Reasoning: Dawn in our study area ranges from 5:45–6:15 AM during 
our sampling period. Using 6:00 introduces less than 30 minutes of 
error, which is acceptable given our 2-hour observation windows.

Alternative considered: Exclude "dawn" entries entirely. Rejected 
because it removes 18% of early-season observations, which would 
bias our temporal analysis toward mid-day.

Trade-off: Slight temporal imprecision in exchange for retaining 
sample size and avoiding seasonal bias.
[0:30–0:32] — What This Does
Notice what this entry does:

It’s transparent — you’re not hiding your reasoning
It shows you thought about alternatives — not just the first thing that came to mind

It acknowledges trade-offs instead of pretending the decision was obvious

This is scientific thinking applied to data work.
Any questions about what a decision log is or why we’d use one? Chat or unmute.




[0:32–0:35] — Setting Up
Okay, now you’re going to practice writing one entry.
I’m going to give you a scenario. You’ll write a decision log entry using the same structure I just showed you.
You’ll have 10 minutes of silent, independent writing time. I’m dropping a Google Doc template in the chat — make your own copy and write in it.
[Drop link in chat]
Don’t worry about perfection. Just practice the structure.




[0:35–0:37]
[Read slowly, give people time to process]:
You’re analyzing bee diversity data from urban gardens. Your dataset includes a column called “Garden Type” with these entries:

Community garden
Community Garden (capital G)
community garden (lowercase)
Comm. garden
School garden
school garden (community-maintained)
Private yard
private yard (open to public)

Your task: Write a decision log entry explaining how you would standardize these categories for analysis — and why.
Questions before we go silent?

[0:37–0:39] — Quick Clarifications
[Answer 1-2 questions if needed]
Great. Silent writing starts now. I’ll mute my mic and play some quiet music. We’ll reconvene at [state exact time].
You can keep your camera on or off — whatever helps you focus.

[0:39–0:49] — SILENT WRITING TIME
[Mute. Optional: play quiet instrumental music. Monitor chat for questions]
[At 5 minutes, briefly unmute]: “You’re halfway. Keep going.”




[0:49–0:52] — Transition
Okay, time’s up. Finish your sentence if you need to, but we’re transitioning.
I’m putting you into breakout rooms of 3 people. Here’s what you’ll do:

Each person reads their entry out loud — just read it, about 1-2 minutes each
After each person reads, the other two give feedback:

One thing that was clear
One place where you wanted more explanation


You’re not grading each other. You’re helping each other see where clarity breaks down.
12 minutes total. About 4 minutes per person. Try to move through all three people.
Questions?

[0:52–0:53] — Send to Breakouts
Great. Sending you out now. See you at [state exact time].

[0:53–1:05] — BREAKOUT ROOMS
[Visit 2-3 rooms briefly]




[1:05–1:08] — Transition Back
Welcome back! That was good work.
I don’t want to hear the specifics of your scenarios right now. Instead, I want to hear:
What made writing hard? What made clarity hard?
Chat or unmute — I want to hear from several of you.

[1:08–1:17] — Harvesting Insights
[Read and respond to 4-5 student observations]:
“I didn’t know how much detail to include.”
Yes. Here’s my guideline: Write enough that a colleague could understand your reasoning without asking follow-up questions. If they’d need you there to explain it, you didn’t write enough.
“I wasn’t sure if my reasoning was good enough.”
Let me reframe that. There’s no such thing as reasoning that’s “good enough” in the abstract. There’s reasoning that’s defensible given your constraints — and reasoning that’s not defensible.
“I combined them because they seemed similar” → not defensible
“I combined community and school gardens into ‘public gardens’ because both involve shared maintenance structures and open access, even though governance differs” → defensible
See the difference?
“I realized I hadn’t thought through alternatives.”
That’s the value of writing it down. Writing reveals what you haven’t thought about yet. That’s not a bug — that’s a feature.
“It was hard to admit trade-offs.”
Yes. Because we’re trained to present conclusions, not uncertainty. But science is trade-offs. Every decision has costs. Pretending they don’t exist doesn’t make your work stronger — it makes it fragile.

[1:17–1:19] — Naming the Core Pattern
Here’s what I’m hearing:
Writing forces you to be explicit about things you thought you’d already decided.
That’s uncomfortable. It’s also essential.
Because when you start coding — which we will soon — you’ll make these same decisions inside filter commands and mutate operations. And if you haven’t written them down, you won’t remember them two weeks later.
Or worse: you won’t be able to defend your own work.




[1:19–1:24] — Making It Practical
Practical question: When do you write in a decision log?
You don’t write every single decision. That would be paralyzing.
You write when:

You’re choosing between two reasonable options (not when the answer is obvious)
You’re combining or recoding categories
You’re excluding data — ALWAYS document exclusions
You’re making an assumption that could be challenged
You tried something and it didn’t work — so future-you doesn’t repeat the mistake

Here’s the test: If someone asked you in a meeting, “Why did you do it that way?” and your honest answer is “Um… I’m not sure,” that’s when you should have written it down.




[1:24–1:32] — Bridging to Workflows
Okay. Decision logs are about recording your reasoning. But they only work if your files and workflow are also reproducible.
Let me show you what I mean.
[Show slide: organized project structure with folders]
This is what a reproducible project looks like:

One folder per project (we’ll use RProjects)
Organized subfolders: raw data, processed data, scripts, figures
Relative file paths so your code works on anyone’s computer

Why does this matter?
Because if I can’t find your data, and I can’t run your code, your decision log is just a story. It’s not reproducible.

[1:32–1:37] — The Workflow Promise
Here’s what we’re building toward this semester:
A way of working where:

Your data stays raw (you never overwrite the original)
Your process is scripted (no manual copy-paste)
Your decisions are documented
Your file paths are robust (they work on my computer, your computer, future-you’s computer)

Today you practiced the decision log. Next week, we’ll build the structure. By Week 3, we’ll start writing actual code inside that structure.
Everything connects.




[1:37–1:39]
Here’s what I want you to do before our next class:

Open R or RStudio on your computer — we sent installation instructions
Just look at the interface. Notice what’s confusing. Notice what’s not.
Open a blank script file. Type your name. Save it. Close it.

That’s it.

[1:39–1:41] — Why I’m Asking This
Why such a simple task?
Because a huge amount of coding anxiety comes from trying to learn the tool and the concepts at the same time.
I want you to get comfortable with what RStudio looks like before we ask it to do anything.
Separate the fears. Tackle them one at a time.




[1:41–1:42]
I’m dropping two links in the chat:

Decision log template — use this all semester
Installation troubleshooting guide — if you hit snags installing R/RStudio





[1:42–1:45]
Before we go, one last thing.
Everything we did today — the writing, the peer review, the struggling with clarity — that’s not “pre-data-science.”
That IS data science.
The coding is just execution. The thinking is the work.
See you next time. Come ready to look at R with curiosity, not fear.
[Stay online for 2-3 minutes for questions]

Slides with decision log example
Slides with organized project structure
Google Doc template for decision log writing
Breakout rooms (groups of 3)
Quiet music (optional, for silent writing)
Decision log template for student download






Silent writing: Some students will finish early. That’s okay. Encourage them to review and refine.
Peer review: Visit rooms and model constructive feedback if needed
Timing: The silent writing section is flexible — can extend to 12 minutes if needed
Backup: If students don’t have R installed yet, that’s okay — the assignment is very low-stakes

text:
Duration: 75 minutes | Online Synchronous | 30 students




Test Zoom/conferencing platform
Prepare Google Doc template for breakout activity
Queue up welcome slide
Have chat window visible
Prepare breakout rooms (groups of 3-4, total 8-10 rooms)





[0:00–0:05] — Arrival and Settling
Good morning, everyone! Welcome to Biology/Chemistry 806. I’m Gretchen LeBuhn, and I’m co-teaching this course with Nicole Adelstein. We’re really glad you’re here.
Before we jump in, let’s take a moment to get settled. Grab water or tea if you need it, adjust your audio settings, and find a comfortable spot. We’re going to be together for 75 minutes, and I want you to feel present and ready to engage.
[Pause 3-4 seconds]
Quick tech check: If you can hear me clearly, give me a thumbs-up reaction or type “yes” in the chat.
Great! If your audio cuts out or something breaks during class, just pop a message in the chat and we’ll sort it out.




[0:05–0:10] — Setting the Tone
Before we dive into activities, I want to be clear about what this course is and what it isn’t.
This is a course about thinking clearly with data.
It’s not about being a coder already. It’s not about memorizing functions or learning statistics in isolation. It’s about learning to explain your reasoning, spot your own assumptions, and revise when something doesn’t make sense.
If you can do that kind of thinking in biology or chemistry, you can do it with data in R. If you struggle to do it in R, that’s not a coding problem — it’s a thinking problem, and we’ll work on it together.
[Pause]
Some of you might be wondering if you belong here. Maybe you’ve never written a line of code. Maybe you’ve used R a little and felt completely lost.
Let me be very clear: prior coding experience is not what matters here.
What matters is whether you’re willing to ask “why,” explain your choices, and revise when things are unclear. That’s science. We’re just applying it to data work.




[0:10–0:13] — Structure Preview
Here’s what we’re doing today:

Get to know each other — not in a forced icebreaker way, but in a way that helps us start noticing patterns in data
Use that process to surface big data science ideas — without touching code yet
Talk about norms — what you want from this class, what I want, and how we’ll work together

I’m not testing you today. I’m watching how you think, not what you already know.
Any questions before we start? You can unmute or use the chat.




[0:13–0:16] — Setting Up the Chat Activity
Okay, first activity. I want everyone to put three things in the chat:

Your name
Your field or program
One kind of data you work with — or hope to work with

If you’re not sure what counts as “data,” that’s totally fine. Just write what comes to mind. If you’ve never worked with data, write that. All answers are useful here.
You’ve got about two minutes. Go ahead and start typing!
[0:16–0:19] — Silent Typing Time
[Monitor chat. If people seem stuck after 30 seconds, you can add: “I’m seeing some great responses coming in. Remember, there’s no wrong answer here.”]

[0:19–0:26] — Reading and Commentary
Okay, I’m going to read some of these out loud — not to put anyone on the spot, but because I want us to start noticing patterns together.
[Read 6-8 responses, pausing to make observations]:

“Excel spreadsheets” — Notice that’s a format, not the phenomenon itself. Interesting distinction.
“Survey responses about student stress” — That’s behavioral data with a specific context.
“I’m not sure” — That’s an important answer too. Uncertainty is data about where we are in our learning.
“Gene sequences” — Molecular data with a very specific structure.

[Pause]
Let’s pause here. We just asked one simple question, and we got very different kinds of answers.
Here’s my question for you — and you can answer in the chat or unmute:
Did everyone interpret “data” the same way?

[0:26–0:30] — Processing Responses
[Read 3-4 chat responses aloud]

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 1: Welcome Back
[0:00–0:03] — Arrival and Settling
Good morning everyone! Welcome to Week 2. How’s everyone doing?
Before we start, quick tech check: If you can hear me, give me a thumbs-up or type “yes” in the chat.
Great! Today we’re talking about projects — not R code, not statistics, but how you organize your work. This might sound boring, but trust me, it’s one of the most important things we’ll cover this semester.
Let me tell you a story. Last year, a graduate student came to me with a failed analysis. She’d spent three weeks coding, and when she tried to run her analysis again after revising one data file, nothing worked. Her paths were all broken, she couldn’t remember which dataset was the “real” one, and she had no documentation of what she’d changed. We had to start over from scratch.
That’s what we’re preventing today.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 2: Last Week Recap
[0:03–0:07] — Connecting to Week 1
Last week, we talked about data science as a way of thinking — about being explicit with your reasoning and documenting your decisions.
We did exercises where you wrote out your analytical thinking in plain language. You described the steps you’d take to clean a dataset, what decisions you’d make, and why.
Here’s the question we didn’t answer: Where do you actually DO that work?
Not in your head. Not in random files scattered across your desktop. You do it in a project.
A project is the basic unit of reproducible scientific work. Everything we do this semester happens inside projects. And I mean everything — every analysis, every figure, every table, every report.
[Pause]
By the end of today’s class, you’ll understand: 1. What a project is and why it matters 2. How to structure project folders 3. Why relative paths are crucial 4. How to document your project so others can use it

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 3: The Messy Desktop Problem
[0:07–0:12] — The Problem
Let me show you something. [Share screen with messy project folder]
This is what a lot of people’s “data analysis” looks like:
Desktop/
├── bee_data_final.csv
├── bee_data_final_FINAL.csv
├── bee_data_final_v2.csv
├── bee_data_v3_USE_THIS_ONE.csv
├── analysis_draft.R
├── analysis_new.R
├── analysis_March15.R
├── richness_plot.png
├── richness_plot_good.png
├── richness_plot_for_paper.png
├── notes.txt
└── meeting_notes_with_advisor.docx
Anyone recognize this pattern? You can admit it — we’ve all been there. I certainly have.
[Pause for chat responses]
Here’s the problem: This structure makes reproducibility impossible.
Let me ask you some questions about this folder:

Which data file is the “real” one? Is it _FINAL? Or _v3_USE_THIS_ONE?
Which script actually generated richness_plot_for_paper.png? Was it analysis_new.R? Or analysis_March15.R?
If I asked you to reproduce this analysis six months from now, where would you even start?
Did you clean the data? Where’s the cleaning script?
Where did bee_data_final.csv come from in the first place? Field data? A collaborator? Downloaded from somewhere?

You can’t answer these questions just by looking at the folder.
And here’s the scary part: If you can’t answer these questions about your own analysis, what hope does a reviewer have? What hope does your future self have?

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 4: Why Projects Matter
[0:10–0:13] — The Core Idea
Here’s the central idea:
A project is a self-contained folder that contains everything needed to reproduce an analysis — data, code, documentation, and outputs — organized in a way that makes sense.
Projects answer three questions:

What data am I using? → stored in data/ folder
What did I do with it? → documented in scripts
What did I produce? → saved in figures/ or outputs/

If someone opens your project folder, they should be able to understand and reproduce your work without asking you questions.
That’s the standard we’re aiming for.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 5: A Well-Organized Project Structure
[0:13–0:17] — The Solution
Here’s what a good project structure looks like:
Biology example:
bee_diversity_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                    # Original field data
│   │   └── bee_surveys.csv
│   └── processed/              # Cleaned data
│       └── bee_clean.csv
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R
│   ├── 02_calculate_richness.R
│   └── 03_make_figures.R
├── figures/
│   └── richness_by_site.png
├── README.md
└── bee_diversity.Rproj
Chemistry example:
pH_titration_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                    # Original instrument output
│   │   └── titration_data.csv
│   └── processed/              # Calibrated data
│       └── pH_corrected.csv
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01_calibration.R
│   ├── 02_calculate_pKa.R
│   └── 03_plot_curves.R
├── figures/
│   └── titration_curve.png
├── README.md
└── pH_analysis.Rproj
[Pause to let students look at this]
Notice a few things:

Clear hierarchy — data, scripts, outputs are separate
Raw data is protected — never modified, only read
Scripts are numbered — you know what order to run them
Self-documenting — folder names tell you what’s inside

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 6: Raw vs. Processed Data
[0:17–0:22] — Critical Distinction
Let’s zoom in on the data folder for a second.
Raw data = what you got from the field, the lab, the instrument, or a collaborator. It never changes.
Processed data = what you created by cleaning or calibrating the raw data. It’s the result of a script.
Biology example: - Raw: Field notebook data with GPS errors, misspelled species names - Processed: Corrected coordinates, standardized species names
Chemistry example: - Raw: Instrument output with baseline drift, uncalibrated readings - Processed: Baseline-corrected, calibrated concentrations
Here’s the rule: You can delete processed data at any time and regenerate it by running your cleaning script.
If you can’t do that — if deleting processed/pH_corrected.csv would break everything — then your workflow is not reproducible.
[Pause]
In the chat, tell me: Have you ever manually edited a dataset in Excel and then saved over the original?
[Wait for responses]
Yeah, we’ve all done it. But that’s a reproducibility disaster. If you edit manually, you can never recreate what you did.
From now on: Raw data is read-only. All changes happen in code.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 7: Relative Paths (The Secret Sauce)
[0:22–0:28] — Why Your Code Must Be Portable
Okay, here’s where things get technical for a second, but this is crucial.
When you write code that reads a file, you need to tell R where the file is. There are two ways to do this:
Absolute path (BAD):
# This only works on Gretchen's computer
data <- read.csv("/Users/gretchen/Desktop/bee_analysis/data/raw/bees.csv")
Relative path (GOOD):
# This works on anyone's computer
data <- read.csv("data/raw/bees.csv")
What’s the difference?
The absolute path only works on my computer. If you try to run my code, it’ll fail because you don’t have a folder called /Users/gretchen/Desktop/....
The relative path works on anyone’s computer as long as they have the project folder, because it’s relative to the project root.
Chemistry example:
# BAD - won't work on your lab partner's computer
titration <- read.csv("C:/Users/Chen/Documents/Lab3/titration.csv")

# GOOD - works for everyone in your lab group
titration <- read.csv("data/raw/titration.csv")
This is what makes projects reproducible.

[0:28–0:32] — Live Demo
Let me show you. [Share screen with RStudio]
I’m going to create a simple project structure for a pH analysis:

Create folder pH_titration/
Inside, create folders: data/raw/, data/processed/, scripts/, figures/
Create an RStudio project: File > New Project > Existing Directory
Create a script: scripts/01_load_data.R
Write: titration_data <- read.csv("data/raw/titration.csv")

Notice that I didn’t write the full path — just "data/raw/titration.csv".
That’s because RStudio automatically sets the working directory to the project folder. All paths are relative to that.
This is why we use RStudio projects for everything.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 8: The README File
[0:32–0:36] — Documentation
Every project needs a README.md file. This is the first thing someone reads when they open your project.
A good README answers:

What is this project about?
What data does it use?
How do I run the analysis? (in what order?)
Who do I contact if I have questions?

Biology example:
# Bee Diversity in Urban Gardens

## Overview
Analysis of bee species richness across 45 urban garden sites 
in San Francisco, 2023-2024.

## Data
- Raw data: `data/raw/bee_surveys.csv` (from field surveys)
- Processed data: `data/processed/bee_clean.csv`

## Analysis
Run scripts in order:
1. `scripts/01_clean_data.R` — removes invalid entries
2. `scripts/02_calculate_richness.R` — calculates rarefied richness
3. `scripts/03_make_figures.R` — generates Figure 1 and Figure 2

## Contact
Gretchen LeBuhn (lebuhn@sfsu.edu)
Chemistry example:
# Acid-Base Titration Analysis

## Overview
Determination of pKa values for unknown organic acids using 
pH titration data from Chem 350L, Fall 2024.

## Data
- Raw data: `data/raw/titration_data.csv` (from pH meter output)
- Processed data: `data/processed/pH_calibrated.csv`

## Analysis
Run scripts in order:
1. `scripts/01_calibration.R` — applies buffer calibration
2. `scripts/02_calculate_pKa.R` — determines pKa from Henderson-Hasselbalch
3. `scripts/03_plot_curves.R` — generates titration curves

## Contact
Nicole Adelstein (nicoleal@sfsu.edu)
Simple. Clear. Reproducible.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
section: SLIDE 9: Breakout Activity — Design a Project Structure
text:
SLIDE 9: Breakout Activity — Design a Project Structure
[0:36–0:38] — Setting Up Breakout Activity
Alright, now you’re going to practice this.
I’m putting you into breakout rooms for 12 minutes. You’ll get one of two scenarios:
Scenario A (Biology): You’re analyzing mercury contamination in fish tissue from 10 coastal sites sampled quarterly for one year. You need to: - Clean the data (remove outliers, standardize units) - Calculate mean mercury concentration by site and season - Compare to EPA safety thresholds - Make a time series plot - Write a short report
Scenario B (Chemistry): You’re analyzing reaction kinetics data from 8 temperature conditions measured every 30 seconds for 10 minutes. You need to: - Clean the data (remove baseline drift) - Calculate rate constants for each temperature - Determine activation energy using Arrhenius equation - Make an Arrhenius plot - Write a short report
Your job: Design a project folder structure for your analysis.

What folders do you need?
What files go where?
What would you name your scripts?
What would your README say?

Write this in the Google Doc I’ll drop in the chat. You don’t need to write code — just plan the structure.
[Drop Google Doc link in chat]

[0:38–0:50] — Breakout Rooms
[Instructor: Circulate through breakout rooms, listen to discussions, offer gentle guidance]
[2 minutes before time’s up: “You have 2 minutes left — start wrapping up your design!”]

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
section: SLIDE 10: Report Out from Breakout Groups
text:
SLIDE 10: Report Out from Breakout Groups
[0:50–1:00] — Whole-Class Discussion
Welcome back! Let’s hear from a few groups.
Group 1 (Biology), what did you come up with?
[Listen, validate good choices, gently correct issues]
Group 3 (Chemistry), show us your structure.
[Listen, validate good choices, gently correct issues]
Common things I’m hearing:

Good: Separation of raw and processed data
Good: Numbered scripts showing order
Good: Clear naming (e.g., 01_calibration.R vs. 01_clean_data.R)
Issue: Some groups put figures in the data folder — outputs should be separate
Issue: Some groups created a “final” folder — there’s no such thing! Everything should regenerate.


[1:00–1:05] — Key Takeaways from Activity
Here’s what I want you to take away from this activity:

Structure forces you to think about workflow — you can’t organize a project until you know what steps you’re taking
Good structure makes collaboration easier — if your lab partner opens your folder, they know where to look
Good structure makes reproducibility possible — six months from now, you’ll know exactly what you did

This isn’t “extra work” that gets in the way of analysis. This IS the analysis.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 11: Common Mistakes
[1:05–1:08] — What to Avoid
Let me tell you about some common mistakes people make:

Mistake 1: Working outside the project folder
If you save files to your Desktop or Documents, they’re not part of the project. Keep everything inside the project folder.


Mistake 2: Using absolute paths
If your code has paths like C:/Users/YourName/..., it won’t run on your lab partner’s computer.


Mistake 3: Editing raw data
Once you bring data into your project, it’s read-only. All changes happen via scripts.
Whether it’s field notebook data or instrument output, protect the original.


Mistake 4: No README
If you don’t document what your project does, future-you will have no idea what’s going on.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 12: Git Setup Preview
[1:08–1:11] — Looking Ahead
Okay, one last thing before we wrap up.
This week’s activity is setting up Git and GitHub. We’re not coding yet — we’re just getting the infrastructure ready.
What is Git?
A version control system that tracks every change you make to your project.
Why do we care?
Because good project structure + version control = fully reproducible, auditable science.
We’ll talk about Git properly in Week 4. For now, just know that your project folders will soon be Git repositories.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 13: Before Next Class
[1:11–1:13] — Homework
Here’s what I want you to do before next class:

Create a project folder for a small analysis (use real data if you have it, or make up a toy example)
Organize it with data/raw/, data/processed/, scripts/, and figures/ folders
Write a README.md file explaining what the project is
Create at least one script (even if it’s just loading data)
Use relative paths — no absolute paths!

That’s it. We’re not analyzing anything yet. We’re just building good habits.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 14: Key Concepts to Remember
[1:13–1:15] — Summary
Let’s review what we covered today:

Projects are the unit of scientific work — not scripts, not sessions
Good structure makes reproducibility possible — data, scripts, outputs are separate
Raw data never changes — all modifications happen via code (whether it’s field data or instrument output)
Relative paths make code portable — so anyone can run your analysis
Documentation matters — README files explain what’s going on

If you get stuck this week, post in the discussion board or come to office hours.
See you Wednesday!
[Stay online for 2-3 minutes for questions]

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
Materials Needed

Messy desktop folder screenshot
Organized project structure diagram
Live demo prepared (RStudio, sample data file)
README examples (good and bad)
Google Doc for breakout activity
Breakout rooms (groups of 3-4)
Exit ticket set up in Canvas/Google Forms

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
Instructor Notes

Timing

The breakout activity is 15 minutes (can extend to 17 if groups need more time)
Exit ticket adds ~2 minutes at end
If running over, can shorten the “common mistakes” section



Common Student Confusion

Raw vs. processed distinction: Students often want to put cleaned data back in raw/. Emphasize that raw means “never modified.”
Absolute vs. relative paths: This is conceptually hard. The live demo helps a lot.
When to use subfolders: Some students create too many subfolders (data/raw/2023/summer/june/). Keep it simple.



Exit Ticket Purpose

Question 1: Checks conceptual understanding
Question 2: Checks understanding of relative vs. absolute paths (common error)
Question 3: Checks ability to apply folder structure to a new scenario

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reproducibility & Decision Logs
Week 1, Day 2

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reproducibility & Decision Logs
Week 1, Day 2

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Welcome Back

Monday: We noticed how ambiguity shows up in simple questions
Today: How do we work with data in ways we can defend, reproduce, and share?

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Monday Was About

When you defined variables like “experience” or “field,” you were making data decisions:

What counts
What doesn’t count
How to measure fuzzy concepts

Those decisions get embedded in your work.
Today’s question: How do we make those decisions visible, defensible, and reproducible?

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Today’s Plan


What is reproducibility?
What is a decision log?
Practice writing one entry
Critique each other’s writing
Connect to project organization

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Sound Familiar?

You work in Excel…
Calculate something…
Copy to Word…
Make a figure…
Paste it…
Email yourself a version…
Save: Analysis_Final_v2_REAL_final.xlsx

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Then Your Advisor Emails

“Can you redo this with the updated data?”
And you think:
“…I have no idea what I did.”

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Is Reproducibility?

Someone else — or future you — can take your data and your process and arrive at the same results.
Not just the same numbers.
The same reasoning.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Three Types of Reproducibility

Computational: Your code runs the same way on different computers
Empirical: Your data collection is documented well enough to repeat
Conceptual: Your decisions are clear enough to understand why
Today’s focus: Conceptual reproducibility

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why This Matters

You’re always collaborating with future-you.
And past-you doesn’t respond to emails.


If you don’t write down why you made a decision: - You won’t remember it in two weeks - You can’t defend it - You can’t reproduce it

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Tool: The Data Decision Log

A running document where you write:

What you decided
Why you decided it
What else you considered
What trade-offs you made

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Example Decision Log Entry

Decision: Converted all “dawn” entries to 6:00 AM.
Reasoning: Dawn in our study area ranges from 5:45–6:15 AM. Using 6:00 introduces <30 minutes of error, acceptable given our 2-hour observation windows.
Alternative considered: Exclude “dawn” entries entirely. Rejected because it removes 18% of early-season observations.
Trade-off: Slight temporal imprecision in exchange for retaining sample size.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What This Entry Does


Transparent — not hiding reasoning
Shows alternatives — not just first idea
Acknowledges trade-offs — doesn’t pretend the decision was obvious

This is scientific thinking applied to data work.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Your Turn: Writing Practice

10 minutes of silent, independent writing
Use the same structure: - Decision - Reasoning - Alternative considered - Trade-off
Google Doc template in chat →

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Scenario

You’re analyzing bee diversity data from urban gardens. Your dataset has a “Garden Type” column with:

Community garden
Community Garden
community garden
Comm. garden
School garden
school garden (community-maintained)
Private yard
private yard (open to public)

Task: Write a decision log entry explaining how you would standardize these categories — and why.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Silent Writing Time

10 minutes
Start now.
(Optional: quiet music)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Peer Review

Breakout rooms of 3 (12 minutes):

Each person reads their entry aloud (1-2 min)
Others give feedback:

One thing that was clear
One place you wanted more explanation


Goal: Help each other see where clarity breaks down

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Made Writing Hard?

Not the specifics of your scenarios—
What made clarity hard?
What made writing difficult?
(Chat or unmute)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“How much detail should I include?”

Guideline:
Write enough that a colleague could understand your reasoning without asking follow-up questions.
If they’d need you there to explain it, you didn’t write enough.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“Is my reasoning good enough?”

There’s no “good enough” in the abstract.
There’s reasoning that’s defensible given your constraints and reasoning that’s not defensible.
Not defensible: “I combined them because they seemed similar”
Defensible: “I combined community and school gardens into ‘public gardens’ because both involve shared maintenance and open access, even though governance structures differ”

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“I hadn’t thought through alternatives”

That’s the value of writing it down.
Writing reveals what you haven’t thought about yet.
That’s not a bug — that’s a feature.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
“It was hard to admit trade-offs”

We’re trained to present conclusions, not uncertainty.
But science IS trade-offs.
Pretending they don’t exist doesn’t make your work stronger—
It makes it fragile.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Core Pattern

Writing forces you to be explicit about things you thought you’d already decided.
That’s uncomfortable.
That’s essential.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
When Do You Use This?

Write in your decision log when:

Choosing between two reasonable options
Combining or recoding categories
Excluding data (ALWAYS)
Making an assumption that could be challenged
Something didn’t work (so future-you doesn’t repeat it)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Test

If someone asked in a meeting:
“Why did you do it that way?”
And your honest answer is:
“Um… I’m not sure”
→ You should have written it down.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
How This Connects to Structure

Decision logs record your reasoning.
But they only work if your files and workflow are also reproducible.
Organized project: - One folder per project (RProject) - Organized subfolders (raw data, processed data, scripts, figures) - Relative file paths (works on anyone’s computer)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Structure Matters

If I can’t find your data
and I can’t run your code,
your decision log is just a story.
It’s not reproducible.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What We’re Building Toward

A way of working where:

Your data stays raw (never overwrite originals)
Your process is scripted (no manual copy-paste)
Your decisions are documented
Your file paths are robust (work on any computer)

Everything connects.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Before Next Class

Low-stakes assignment:

Open R or RStudio
Just look at the interface
Open a blank script file
Type your name
Save it
Close it

That’s it.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Such a Simple Task?

Coding anxiety comes from learning the tool and the concepts at the same time.
Get comfortable with what RStudio looks like before we ask it to do anything.
Separate the fears. Tackle them one at a time.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Resources

In the chat:

Decision log template (use all semester)
R/RStudio installation troubleshooting guide

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Final Thought

Everything we did today — writing, peer review, struggling with clarity —
That’s not “pre-data-science.”
That IS data science.
The coding is just execution.
The thinking is the work.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
See you next time!
Come ready to look at R with curiosity, not fear.

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text: Duration: 75 minutes | Format: Online Synchronous | Students: 30

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
Pre-Class Setup (Instructor)

Test Zoom/conferencing platform
Prepare examples of bad and good pseudocode (biology and chemistry)
Have Week 1 analysis descriptions ready to reference
Prepare Google Doc for guided exercise
Prepare breakout rooms (groups of 3-4)
Queue up examples of ambiguous instructions

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 1: Welcome
[0:00–0:03] — Arrival and Settling
Good morning! Welcome to Day 2 of Week 2.
Quick tech check: If you can hear me and see the slides, give me a thumbs-up.
Today we’re talking about pseudocode. If that word sounds intimidating, don’t worry — pseudocode is just a fancy name for “writing down what you plan to do before you do it.”

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 2: Last Class Recap
[0:03–0:06] — Connecting to Monday
On Monday, we talked about organizing projects — folders, file structures, relative paths, README files.
Today, we’re zooming in one level: How do you plan what goes inside those scripts?
You can have the best folder structure in the world, but if your scripts are a mess of unplanned commands, your analysis won’t be reproducible.
Pseudocode is the bridge between scientific thinking and code.

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 3: What Is Pseudocode?
[0:06–0:10] — Definition
Pseudocode is a step-by-step description of what you want your code to do, written in plain language.
It’s not code. It’s not prose. It’s something in between.
Think of it as a recipe for analysis:

Clear enough that someone could follow it
Specific enough that there’s no ambiguity
General enough that you’re not writing actual code yet

Here are examples from both fields:
Biology - Bad (too vague): - “Clean the species data”
Biology - Better (pseudocode): - “Remove rows where species name is missing” - “Remove rows where species name contains obvious typos (checked against species list)” - “Standardize species names to match taxonomy database” - “Save cleaned data to data/processed/species_clean.csv”
Chemistry - Bad (too vague): - “Process the spectroscopy data”
Chemistry - Better (pseudocode): - “Load absorbance data from CSV file” - “Subtract baseline absorbance (measured at 800 nm)” - “Apply Beer-Lambert law to calculate concentrations” - “Remove concentrations outside calibration range (0-10 μM)” - “Save processed data to data/processed/concentrations.csv”
See the difference?

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 4: Why Pseudocode Matters
[0:10–0:14] — The Case for Planning
Why do we need pseudocode? Three reasons:
1. It forces you to think before you code
Most coding mistakes happen because people start typing before they know what they’re trying to do. Pseudocode makes you slow down and plan.
2. It reveals ambiguity
When you write “clean the data,” you think you know what you mean. But when you try to write pseudocode, you realize: What does “clean” mean? What counts as invalid? What do I do with missing values?
Biology example: “Remove outliers” — which outliers? Based on what criteria? Standard deviations? IQR? Domain knowledge?
Chemistry example: “Correct for drift” — linear drift? Exponential? What’s your baseline reference?
Pseudocode surfaces those questions before you waste time coding.
3. It makes collaboration easier
If you write pseudocode, someone else can review your logic before you invest hours in coding. You can catch flawed reasoning early.
[Pause]
Here’s the key insight: Good pseudocode can be translated into any programming language.
If your pseudocode is clear, converting it to R is almost mechanical. If your pseudocode is vague, your code will be vague too.

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
section: SLIDE 5: Pseudocode vs. Code vs. Prose
text:
SLIDE 5: Pseudocode vs. Code vs. Prose
[0:14–0:18] — Three Modes of Thinking
Let’s look at the same task written three ways:
Chemistry example:
Prose (too informal): > “I’m going to remove the bad absorbance readings and then calculate the concentrations using the calibration curve.”
Pseudocode (just right): - Load absorbance data from instrument output - Remove rows where absorbance is negative (instrument error) - Remove rows where absorbance > 3.0 (out of linear range) - Apply calibration equation: concentration = (absorbance - 0.05) / 0.123 - Create scatterplot of concentration vs. time - Save plot to figures/concentration_timeseries.png
Code (too specific):
data <- read.csv("data/raw/absorbance.csv")
data_clean <- data %>% 
  filter(absorbance >= 0,
         absorbance <= 3.0) %>%
  mutate(concentration = (absorbance - 0.05) / 0.123)
ggplot(data_clean, aes(x = time, y = concentration)) +
  geom_point()
ggsave("figures/concentration_timeseries.png")
[Pause]
Notice that pseudocode has: - Verbs — “Load,” “Remove,” “Apply,” “Create,” “Save” - Specific conditions — “where absorbance is negative,” “absorbance > 3.0” - Clear outputs — “scatterplot,” “save to figures/” - Domain knowledge — “out of linear range,” “calibration equation”
It’s detailed enough to be unambiguous, but general enough that you’re not worrying about syntax.

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 6: Common Pseudocode Mistakes
[0:18–0:22] — What to Avoid
Let me show you some common mistakes people make when writing pseudocode.

Mistake 1: Too vague
Biology example: ❌ “Standardize the measurements”
That could mean anything. Be specific about what you’re standardizing and how.
✅ “Divide each bird mass by wing length to get body condition index”
Chemistry example: ❌ “Normalize the data”
What kind of normalization?
✅ “Divide each absorbance value by the maximum absorbance to scale from 0 to 1”



Mistake 2: Too detailed (actually writing code)
Biology example: ❌ “Use filter() to subset where count >= 5”
That’s code, not pseudocode. You’re worrying about syntax before you’ve clarified the logic.
✅ “Remove sites with fewer than 5 observations”
Chemistry example: ❌ “Use mutate() to create new column with pH = -log10(H_concentration)”
✅ “Calculate pH from hydrogen ion concentration”



Mistake 3: Skipping steps
Biology example: ❌ “Load field data, make species accumulation curve”
What happened in between? Did you clean it? Aggregate by site? Calculate richness?
✅ “Load field data → Remove incomplete surveys → Count species per site → Calculate cumulative species richness → Plot accumulation curve”
Chemistry example: ❌ “Load titration data, determine pKa”
Too many hidden steps!
✅ “Load pH and volume data → Identify equivalence point → Calculate half-equivalence pH → Report pKa value”



Mistake 4: No decision points
Biology example: ❌ “Remove rare species”
How do you define rare? What’s your cutoff?
✅ “Remove species that occur in fewer than 3 sites (less than 10% of total sites)”
Chemistry example: ❌ “Remove bad datapoints”
What makes a datapoint “bad”?
✅ “Remove datapoints where pH meter error flag is TRUE or pH change > 2 units between consecutive readings”
[Pause]
The pattern here: Good pseudocode makes all decisions explicit.

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 7: Let’s Practice Together
[0:22–0:28] — Guided Exercise
Alright, let’s practice. I’m going to give you a scenario, and we’ll write pseudocode together.
Scenario (Biology/Ecology):
You have a dataset of bird observations. Each row has: - Species name - Date of observation - Location (latitude/longitude) - Observer name
You want to: 1. Count how many observations there are for each species 2. Create a bar chart showing the 10 most commonly observed species 3. Save the chart
[Pause]
Let’s build this step by step. I’ll start, and you can type suggestions in the chat.
Here’s how I’d start:
STEP 1: Load the bird observation data
What comes next? Type in the chat — what’s the next step?
[Wait for responses]

[0:28–0:32] — Collaborative Building
Great! I’m seeing: - “Count observations per species” - “Group by species and count” - “Summarize by species”
Those are all getting at the same idea. Let me write it in pseudocode:
STEP 1: Load the bird observation data
STEP 2: Count the number of observations for each species
Good. Now what? We want the top 10. How do we get those?
[Wait for responses]
Right! We need to sort and take the top 10:
STEP 1: Load the bird observation data
STEP 2: Count the number of observations for each species
STEP 3: Sort species by count (highest to lowest)
STEP 4: Keep only the top 10 species
Now we need to make the plot. What kind of plot?
[Wait for responses]
Bar chart, yes:
STEP 5: Create a bar chart with species on x-axis, count on y-axis
And finally?
STEP 6: Save the chart to figures/top_species.png

[0:32–0:36] — Analysis of Our Pseudocode
Let’s look at what we just wrote:
STEP 1: Load the bird observation data
STEP 2: Count the number of observations for each species
STEP 3: Sort species by count (highest to lowest)
STEP 4: Keep only the top 10 species
STEP 5: Create a bar chart with species on x-axis, count on y-axis
STEP 6: Save the chart to figures/top_species.png
Is this good pseudocode? Let’s check:
✅ Clear verbs — Load, Count, Sort, Keep, Create, Save
✅ Specific steps — We know exactly what’s happening
✅ Ordered logically — Each step depends on the previous one
✅ Not code — We didn’t worry about R syntax
✅ Explicit output — We know where the file is saved
This pseudocode could be translated into R, Python, or even Excel. The logic is clear.

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 8: Identifying Ambiguity in Pseudocode
[0:36–0:42] — Debugging Bad Pseudocode
Now let’s look at some pseudocode that has problems. I want you to spot the ambiguity.
Example 1 (Chemistry):
Load the titration dataset
Clean the pH data
Calculate the equivalence point
Plot the titration curve
What’s wrong with this? Type in the chat.
[Wait for responses]
Exactly! It’s way too vague. What does “clean” mean? How do you calculate equivalence point? What kind of plot?

Example 2 (Biology):
Load temperature data from field sensors
Remove outliers
Calculate average temperature by site
Make a plot
Better, but still problems. What’s ambiguous here?
[Wait for responses]
Right! How do we define outliers? Are we using standard deviations? Domain knowledge? And what kind of plot?
Here’s a better version:
Load temperature data from field sensors
Remove temperatures below -50°C or above 60°C (sensor error range)
Remove temperatures more than 3 standard deviations from site mean
Calculate mean temperature for each site
Create a bar plot of mean temperature by site (ordered north to south)
Save plot to figures/temp_by_site.png
Much clearer!

Example 3 (Chemistry):
Load absorbance spectra
Correct for baseline
Find peak wavelength
Save results
What’s missing here?
[Wait for responses]
Better version:
Load absorbance spectra from UV-Vis instrument
Subtract minimum absorbance (wavelength 800-900 nm) from all values
Identify wavelength with maximum absorbance in range 400-700 nm
Extract absorbance value at peak wavelength
Save wavelength and absorbance to data/processed/peak_data.csv

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
section: SLIDE 9: Breakout Activity — Rewrite Your Week 1 Analysis
text:
SLIDE 9: Breakout Activity — Rewrite Your Week 1 Analysis
[0:42–0:45] — Setting Up
Okay, now it’s your turn.
In Week 1, you wrote a plain-language description of an analysis: clean a dataset with missing and invalid values, summarize it, and produce a figure.
Now you’re going to rewrite that description as formal pseudocode.
I’m sending you to breakout rooms for 15 minutes. Here’s what I want:

Rewrite your Week 1 analysis as numbered pseudocode steps
Be specific — no vague verbs like “clean” or “summarize”
Make decisions explicit — if you’re removing something, say what and why
Include domain-specific details (e.g., “temperatures below -50°C,” “pH > 14,” “absorbance < 0”)
Write it in the Google Doc I’ll drop in the chat

When you’re done, you’ll have pseudocode that could be handed to someone else and they’d know exactly what to do.
[Drop Google Doc link in chat]

[0:45–1:00] — Breakout Rooms
[Instructor: Circulate through rooms, check in, offer feedback]
[2 minutes before end: “You have 2 minutes — wrap up your pseudocode!”]

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:
SLIDE 10: Report Out
[1:00–1:08] — Whole-Class Sharing
Welcome back! Let’s see what you came up with.
[Call on 2-3 groups to share their pseudocode]
Group 2 (Chemistry), can you walk us through your pseudocode?
[Listen, validate good choices, gently point out remaining ambiguities]
Group 5 (Biology), what did you come up with?
[Listen, validate good choices, gently point out remaining ambiguities]

[1:08–1:12] — Common Patterns
Here’s what I’m noticing across groups:
Good: - Most of you specified what counts as invalid (e.g., “temperature below 0°C,” “negative absorbance values”) - Most of you ordered your steps logically - Most of you specified output file names and locations - Good use of domain knowledge (measurement ranges, physical constraints)
Needs work: - A few groups still have vague verbs like “process” or “analyze” — be more specific! - Some groups skipped intermediate steps — don’t assume the reader knows what you mean - A few groups mixed pseudocode with actual code syntax — stay in plain language
Chemistry-specific observation: - Great job being specific about units and calibration steps! - Remember to document your equations (e.g., “Apply Beer-Lambert law: A = εbc”)
Biology-specific observation: - Good job considering data quality checks (GPS errors, taxonomic issues) - Remember to document your grouping decisions (e.g., “aggregate by site,” “summarize by month”)

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
section: SLIDE 11: Pseudocode as a Tool for Debugging
text:
SLIDE 11: Pseudocode as a Tool for Debugging
[1:12–1:15] — Beyond Planning
Here’s something I want you to remember:
Pseudocode isn’t just for planning. It’s also for debugging.
When your code isn’t working, the problem is usually one of two things:

Your logic is flawed — you’re asking the computer to do the wrong thing
Your syntax is wrong — you’re asking correctly but using the wrong words

If you have pseudocode, you can separate these problems:

Go back to your pseudocode and ask: “Is this what I actually want to do?”
If the pseudocode is right but the code is wrong, it’s a syntax problem (easier to fix with Google/ChatGPT)
If the pseudocode is wrong, fix the logic first, then rewrite the code

Chemistry example: - Pseudocode says: “Calculate molarity from mass and volume” - But you forgot: “First convert mass to moles using molecular weight” - That’s a logic error, not a syntax error!
Biology example: - Pseudocode says: “Calculate species richness per site” - But you forgot: “First remove duplicate observations of same species at same site” - Fix the logic, then fix the code!
This saves hours of frustration.

title: Week 2, Day 2: Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
text:

Here’s what I want you to do before Monday:
Exit Ticket:
Write pseudocode for ONE of these tasks (choose based on your field):
Option A (Biology/Ecology): > You have a dataset of plant heights measured at different light levels. Read the dataset, remove plants with negative height values (data entry errors), remove plants with height > 300 cm (measurement errors), calculate the mean height for each light level, and save the summary to a new file.
Option B (Chemistry): > You have UV-Vis absorbance data from a kinetics experiment. Read the dataset, subtract the baseline absorbance (first 5 timepoints), remove any absorbance values < 0 or > 3 (outside linear range), calculate the slope of absorbance vs. time (reaction rate), and save the rate constant to a new file.

text:
SLIDE 13: Key Takeaways
[1:15] — Summary
Let’s review what we covered:

Pseudocode is a planning tool — it bridges scientific thinking and code
Good pseudocode is specific, ordered, and explicit — no ambiguity
Pseudocode reveals flawed logic before you waste time coding
Pseudocode is language-agnostic — it can be translated into any programming language
Use domain knowledge in pseudocode — measurement ranges, physical constraints, scientific decisions

Next week: We’ll start writing actual code inside Quarto documents. But the pseudocode you write this week will make that much easier.

text:
The Messy Desktop Problem

Desktop/
├── bee_data_final.csv
├── bee_data_final_FINAL.csv
├── bee_data_v3_USE_THIS_ONE.csv
├── analysis_draft.R

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Problem with Messy Projects

Can you reproduce your analysis six months from now?

Which data file is the real one?
Which script actually generated the plot?
What order do things run in?
Where did the data come from?

You can’t answer these questions just by looking at the folder.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Projects Matter

A project is a self-contained folder that contains everything needed to reproduce an analysis.
Projects answer three questions:

What data am I using? → data/ folder
What did I do with it? → documented in scripts
What did I produce? → saved in figures/ or outputs/

Standard: Someone should be able to understand and reproduce your work without asking questions.

A Well-Organized Project

bee_diversity_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                # Original, untouched
│   │   ├── bee_surveys_2023.csv

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Raw vs. Processed Data

data/
├── raw/         # What you started with
└── processed/   # What you created


Raw data = from field/lab/instrument/collaborator
→ Never changes. Ever.
Processed data = created by cleaning/transforming raw data
→ Result of running a script
Golden rule:
You can delete all processed data and regenerate it by running your scripts.

text:

Absolute path (BAD):
data <- read.csv("/Users/gretchen/Desktop/bees.csv")

data <- read.csv("data/raw/bees.csv")
Works on anyone’s computer!
This is what makes projects reproducible.
