title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 4: The Cost of Disorganization
[0:12–0:15] — Real Consequences
Let me tell you what happens with disorganized projects:
Scenario 1: The Reviewer Requests Changes
A reviewer asks you to re-run your analysis excluding one site that might be contaminated. You open your project six months later. Which script do you run? Which data file do you use? You end up redoing the entire analysis because you can’t figure out what you did the first time.
Scenario 2: Your Lab Partner Needs Your Data
Your lab partner wants to build on your work. You send them your folder. They try to run your script and get an error: Error: cannot open file 'C:/Users/YourName/Desktop/data.csv'. The path is hardcoded to your computer. They have to manually fix every file path.
Scenario 3: You Want to Publish Your Data and Code
A journal requires you to deposit your data and code in a repository. You try to package it up. You realize you have no README, no documentation, no explanation of what anything means. You spend a week writing documentation for code you barely remember writing.
[Pause]
All of these problems are solved by one thing: A well-organized project.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 5: What Is a Project?
[0:15–0:18] — Core Definition
Here’s the central idea:
A project is a self-contained folder that contains everything needed to reproduce an analysis — data, code, documentation, and outputs — organized in a way that makes sense to someone else.
Let me unpack that:
Self-contained = All files are inside one folder. Nothing lives on your Desktop. Nothing lives in random Downloads folders.
Everything needed = Data, scripts, outputs, documentation. If it’s part of the analysis, it’s in the project.
Organized in a way that makes sense = Clear folder structure. Logical file names. Obvious ordering.
To someone else = Not just to you. To a collaborator. To a reviewer. To your future self.
Projects answer three questions:

What data am I using? → stored in data/ folder
What did I do with it? → documented in scripts
What did I produce? → saved in figures/ or outputs/

If someone opens your project folder, they should be able to understand and reproduce your work without asking you questions.
That’s the standard we’re aiming for.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 6: A Well-Organized Project Structure
[0:18–0:23] — The Solution
Here’s what a good project structure looks like:
bee_diversity_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                    # Original, untouched data
│   │   ├── bee_surveys_2023.csv
│   │   └── site_characteristics.csv
│   └── processed/              # Cleaned data (never edit raw!)
│       ├── bee_clean.csv
│       └── sites_clean.csv
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R         # Numbered = order to run
│   ├── 02_calculate_richness.R
│   └── 03_make_figures.R
├── figures/
│   ├── richness_by_site.png
│   └── accumulation_curve.png
├── outputs/
│   └── richness_summary.csv
├── README.md                    # START HERE
├── .gitignore                   # Files to ignore (we'll cover this later)
└── bee_diversity.Rproj          # RStudio project file
[Pause to let students look at this]
Let’s walk through what makes this good:
1. Clear hierarchy - Data is separate from scripts - Scripts are separate from outputs - Each folder has one job
2. Raw data is protected - Original data never changes - It’s in its own raw/ subfolder - All modifications happen via scripts
3. Scripts are numbered - You know the order to run them - 01_ runs before 02_ runs before 03_ - No guessing
4. Self-documenting - Folder names tell you what’s inside - File names are descriptive - README explains the project
5. Outputs are separate - Figures go in figures/ - Tables or summaries go in outputs/ - Nothing gets lost in the scripts/ folder

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
section: SLIDE 7: Deep Dive — The Data Folder
text:
SLIDE 7: Deep Dive — The Data Folder
[0:23–0:28] — Critical Distinction
Let’s zoom in on the most important part of project structure: the data folder.
data/
├── raw/         # What you started with
└── processed/   # What you created
This distinction is fundamental to reproducibility.
Raw data = what you got from the field, the lab, an instrument, a collaborator, or a database. It never changes. Ever.
Processed data = what you created by cleaning, filtering, transforming, or combining the raw data. It’s the result of running a script.
Here’s the golden rule:

You can delete all processed data at any time and regenerate it by running your scripts.

If you can’t do that — if deleting processed/bee_clean.csv would break everything — then your workflow is not reproducible.
Let me give you examples:
Biology example: - Raw: Field notebook data with GPS errors, misspelled species names, missing dates - Processed: Corrected coordinates, standardized species names, filled dates based on field notes - How to regenerate: Run 01_clean_data.R which loads raw/field_data.csv and creates processed/field_clean.csv
Chemistry example: - Raw: pH meter output with baseline drift, uncalibrated readings, instrument artifacts - Processed: Baseline-corrected values, calibrated to buffer standards, artifacts removed - How to regenerate: Run 01_calibration.R which loads raw/ph_raw.csv and creates processed/ph_calibrated.csv
[Pause]
In the chat, tell me: Have you ever manually edited a dataset in Excel and then saved over the original?
[Wait 10 seconds for responses]
[Read some responses aloud]
Yeah, we’ve all done it. But that’s a reproducibility disaster. If you manually change cell C45 from 3.2 to 3.5 because “it looked wrong,” and then save the file, you can never recreate what you did.
Was it a typo? A measurement error? A calculation error? Did you change other cells too? Nobody will ever know.
From now on: Raw data is read-only. All changes happen in code.
This is hard at first. You’ll want to “quickly fix” something in Excel. Don’t do it. Write the code instead.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 8: Relative Paths (The Secret Sauce)
[0:28–0:34] — Why Your Code Must Be Portable
Okay, here’s where things get technical for a second, but this is crucial.
When you write code that reads a file, you need to tell R where the file is. There are two ways to do this:
Absolute path (BAD):
# This only works on MY computer
data <- read.csv("/Users/gretchen/Desktop/bee_analysis/data/raw/bees.csv")
Relative path (GOOD):
# This works on ANYONE's computer
data <- read.csv("data/raw/bees.csv")
What’s the difference?
The absolute path includes the full location from the root of your computer: /Users/gretchen/Desktop/...
This only works on my computer. If you try to run my code, it will fail with an error like:
Error: cannot open file '/Users/gretchen/Desktop/bee_analysis/data/raw/bees.csv': 
No such file or directory
Why? Because you don’t have a user named “gretchen” on your computer. Even if you download my project folder, the path won’t exist for you.
The relative path is relative to the project folder: data/raw/bees.csv
This means: “Starting from wherever the project is located, go into the data folder, then the raw subfolder, and read bees.csv.”
As long as you have the project folder with that structure, the code will work. It doesn’t matter if the project is on your Desktop, in your Documents, on an external drive, or on someone else’s computer.
This is what makes projects portable and reproducible.

[0:34–0:38] — Why This Matters
Let me give you a concrete scenario:
You finish your analysis on your computer at school. You organize it beautifully, but you use absolute paths in all your code:
data <- read.csv("C:/Users/Student/Documents/Research/data.csv")
You go home. You want to keep working on your laptop. You copy the project folder to your laptop.
You try to run your script. ERROR. Because your laptop doesn’t have C:/Users/Student/Documents/...
You manually change all the paths. Now it works on your laptop.
You go back to school. ERROR. Because you changed the paths and now they don’t work on your school computer.
You email your advisor your analysis. She tries to run it. ERROR. Because she doesn’t have your folder structure.
See the problem? Absolute paths make your code fragile. It breaks as soon as you move it.
Relative paths make your code robust. Move the project anywhere. Share it with anyone. It still works.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
section: SLIDE 9: Live Demo — Creating an RStudio Project
text:
SLIDE 9: Live Demo — Creating an RStudio Project
[0:38–0:44] — Hands-On Demonstration
Alright, let me show you how to actually create a project in RStudio.
[Share screen with RStudio]
I’m going to create a simple project structure from scratch. Follow along visually — you’ll do this yourself for your homework.
Step 1: Create the project folder
I’ll use Finder (Mac) or File Explorer (Windows) to create a new folder. I’m calling it water_quality_analysis.
water_quality_analysis/    [Created manually]
Step 2: Create subfolders
Inside that folder, I create these folders: - data - Inside data, I create raw and processed - scripts - figures
water_quality_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
├── scripts/
└── figures/
Step 3: Add a data file
I’ll copy a sample dataset into data/raw/. Let’s say I have water_samples.csv.
water_quality_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── water_samples.csv    [Added]
│   └── processed/
├── scripts/
└── figures/
Step 4: Create an RStudio Project
Now I open RStudio and go to File > New Project.
I select Existing Directory (because I already created the folder).
I navigate to water_quality_analysis and click Create Project.
RStudio creates a file called water_quality_analysis.Rproj.
water_quality_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   │   └── water_samples.csv
│   └── processed/
├── scripts/
├── figures/
└── water_quality_analysis.Rproj    [Created by RStudio]
Step 5: Create a script with relative paths
I create a new R script: File > New File > R Script.
I’ll save it as scripts/01_load_data.R.
Inside, I write:
# Load water quality data
water <- read.csv("data/raw/water_samples.csv")

# Check that it loaded
head(water)
Notice: The path is "data/raw/water_samples.csv" — it’s relative to the project folder.
Step 6: Test it
I run the code. It works!
Now watch this: I’ll close RStudio completely. I’ll move the entire water_quality_analysis folder to my Desktop.
I double-click the .Rproj file. RStudio opens the project.
I run the script again. It still works.
Why? Because the path is relative. As long as the folder structure inside the project is intact, the code runs anywhere.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 10: The README File
[0:44–0:49] — Documentation is Part of the Project
Every project needs a README.md file. This is the first thing someone reads when they open your project.
A good README answers four questions:

What is this project about?
What data does it use?
How do I run the analysis? (What order do I run scripts?)
Who do I contact if I have questions?

Let me show you a good README and a bad README.
Bad README:
# My Project

This is my analysis.
That’s useless. It tells me nothing.
Good README:
# Bee Diversity in Urban Gardens

## Overview
This project analyzes bee species richness across 45 urban garden sites 
in San Francisco, sampled May–August 2023.

Research question: Does species richness differ between community gardens 
and private yards?

## Data
- Raw data: `data/raw/bee_surveys.csv` (field surveys from summer 2023)
- Processed data: `data/processed/bee_clean.csv` (created by `01_clean_data.R`)

## Scripts
Run scripts in this order:

1. `scripts/01_clean_data.R` 
   - Removes incomplete surveys (missing site ID or date)
   - Standardizes species names to match BugGuide taxonomy
   - Creates `data/processed/bee_clean.csv`

2. `scripts/02_calculate_richness.R`
   - Calculates rarefied richness standardized to 3 surveys per site
   - Uses the vegan package
   - Creates `outputs/richness_by_site.csv`

3. `scripts/03_make_figures.R`
   - Generates Figure 1 (richness by garden type)
   - Saves to `figures/richness_comparison.png`

I could hand this to a reviewer, and they’d know exactly how to reproduce my analysis.

text:
SLIDE 11: Breakout Activity — Design a Project Structure
[0:49–0:51] — Setting Up Breakout Activity
Alright, now you’re going to practice designing a project structure.
I’m putting you into breakout rooms for 15 minutes. Here’s your scenario:
Scenario: You’re analyzing water quality data from 10 sites sampled monthly for one year. You measured pH, dissolved oxygen, and nitrate concentration. You need to: - Clean the data (remove sensor errors outside valid ranges) - Calculate monthly averages for each site - Compare sites to EPA water quality standards - Make a time series plot showing trends over the year - Write a short summary report
Your job: 1. Design a complete project folder structure 2. Name all the folders and subfolders 3. List what files would go in each folder 4. Decide on script names and their order 5. Write a brief README outline
Write your design in the Google Doc I’m dropping in the chat. Don’t write any code — just plan the structure.
Questions to guide your thinking: - What goes in data/raw/? - What goes in data/processed/? - How many scripts do you need? - What should they be named? - What outputs will you create?
[Drop Google Doc link in chat]
Work together in your groups. I’ll visit rooms to see how you’re doing.

[0:51–1:06] — Breakout Rooms
[Instructor: Circulate through breakout rooms every 3-4 minutes]
[Listen to discussions, offer hints if groups are stuck]
[Common places groups get stuck: deciding how many scripts they need, or what to name processed data files]
[2 minutes before end: “You have 2 minutes left — wrap up your design and make sure someone can present it!”]

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
section: SLIDE 12: Report Out from Breakout Groups
text:
SLIDE 12: Report Out from Breakout Groups
[1:06–1:15] — Whole-Class Discussion
Welcome back! That was great work. Let’s hear from a few groups.
Group 3, can you share your structure? Someone unmute and walk us through what you decided.
[Listen to Group 3’s structure]
[Validate good choices, gently correct issues]
For example: - “I love that you separated raw and processed data — that’s crucial.” - “I see you created data/EPA_standards.csv — where does that go? Is it raw data or reference data? Maybe create a data/reference/ folder?” - “You have three scripts — great! But can someone else tell what order to run them just from the names? Consider adding numbers: 01_clean.R, 02_analyze.R, 03_plot.R.”

Group 7, what did you come up with? Different from Group 3?
[Listen to Group 7’s structure]
[Compare the two approaches]
Interesting! So Group 3 put all cleaning in one script, and Group 7 split it into two scripts: one for removing errors, one for calculating averages. Both approaches can work! The key is that your README explains what each script does.

[1:15–1:18] — Synthesizing Common Patterns
Let me summarize what I saw across most groups:
Things most groups got right: 1. ✅ Separated data/raw/ and data/processed/ 2. ✅ Numbered scripts to show order 3. ✅ Created a figures/ folder for plots 4. ✅ Named scripts descriptively (clean_data.R, not script1.R)
Common issues I saw: 1. ❌ Some groups created a final_outputs/ folder — don’t do this! Everything should be reproducible. There’s no “final” until the paper is published. 2. ❌ Some groups weren’t sure whether to put EPA standards in raw/ or processed/ — if you downloaded it from EPA and didn’t modify it, it’s raw! 3. ❌ Some groups forgot to plan for a README — always document your project!
Key insight from this exercise:
You can’t design a good project structure until you understand your analytical workflow. That’s why we spent last week and today thinking about planning before coding.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 13: Common Mistakes to Avoid
[1:18–1:22] — Learning from Others’ Errors
Let me tell you about common mistakes I see students make with projects:

Mistake 1: Working outside the project folder
You’re working on your analysis. You make a quick plot just to check something. You save it to your Desktop.
Later, you want to include that plot in your paper. Where did you save it? Was it plot1.png or figure_temp.png? Did you already delete it?
Rule: If it’s part of the analysis, it goes in the project folder. No exceptions.



Mistake 2: Using absolute paths
You write a script with absolute paths:
data <- read.csv("C:/Users/YourName/School/Research/Fall2024/data.csv")
You share it with your lab partner. They run it. Error.
Why? Because they don’t have C:/Users/YourName/School/... on their computer.
Rule: Always use relative paths. Always.



Mistake 3: Editing raw data
You open data/raw/field_data.csv in Excel. You notice row 47 has a typo. You fix it. You save the file.
Congratulations, you just destroyed reproducibility. Now nobody knows what you changed, not even you when you look at this six months from now.
Rule: Raw data is read-only. If you need to fix something, write code to fix it. Add a comment explaining why.
Example:
# Remove row 47 - field notes indicate this was a data entry error
# Observer confirmed species was actually "Bombus vosnesenskii", not "Bомbus" (Cyrillic character)
data_clean <- data %>% filter(row_number() != 47)



Mistake 4: No README
You finish your analysis. You put everything in folders. It looks great!
Six months later, you open the project. You have no idea what 02_analysis_v3.R does differently from 02_analysis_v2.R.
Your advisor asks to see your analysis. She opens the project. She has no idea where to start.
Rule: Write your README as you go. Update it when you change things. Future-you will thank present-you.



Mistake 5: Too many versions
You’re worried about breaking your code. So you save multiple versions: - analysis.R - analysis_v2.R - analysis_final.R - analysis_final_fixed.R - analysis_final_fixed_really.R
This is what version control (Git) solves. We’ll cover that in Week 4. For now, just know: you shouldn’t have multiple versions of the same script in your project.

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 14: The Project Checklist
[1:22–1:25] — Quick Reference
Here’s a checklist for a good project structure. Every project you create this semester should have:
Folder Structure: - [ ] data/raw/ — original data, never modified - [ ] data/processed/ — cleaned/transformed data - [ ] scripts/ — numbered R scripts showing order - [ ] figures/ — all plots and visualizations - [ ] outputs/ — tables, summaries, or other results (optional)
Files: - [ ] .Rproj file — makes it an RStudio project - [ ] README.md — explains what the project does - [ ] Descriptive file names (not analysis.R or data.csv)
Code Practices: - [ ] Relative paths only (never absolute paths) - [ ] Scripts are numbered if order matters - [ ] Comments explain decisions - [ ] Raw data is never modified
Documentation: - [ ] README explains research question - [ ] README lists data sources - [ ] README explains how to run the analysis - [ ] README includes contact information

title: Week 2, Day 1: Projects as the Unit of Scientific Work
text:
SLIDE 15: Git Setup Preview
[1:25–1:28] — Looking Ahead
One last thing before we finish: this week’s activity is setting up Git and GitHub.
What is Git? A version control system that tracks every change you make to your files. Think of it as “Track Changes” for your entire project.
What is GitHub? A website where you can host your Git repositories online and collaborate with others.
Why do we care? Because good project structure + version control = fully reproducible, auditable science.
Instead of having files named analysis_final_REALLY_final_v3.R, you’ll have a single file called analysis.R and Git will track all the versions for you.
We’ll cover Git concepts properly in Week 4. For now, just get it installed and set up. The activity instructions are on Canvas.

text:
SLIDE 18: Key Concepts to Remember
[After exit ticket] — Summary
Let’s review the main concepts from today:

Projects are the unit of scientific work — not scripts, not sessions, not random files
Good structure makes reproducibility possible — data, scripts, and outputs are clearly separated
Raw data never changes — all modifications happen via code in scripts
Relative paths make code portable — so anyone can run your analysis anywhere
Documentation is not optional — README files explain your project to others (and to future-you)
Organization is part of doing science — it’s not extra work, it IS the work

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Cost of Disorganization

Scenario 1: Reviewer requests changes
→ Can’t figure out what you did 6 months later
Scenario 2: Lab partner needs your data
→ Error: cannot open 'C:/Users/YourName/...'
Scenario 3: Journal requires code deposit
→ Week of writing documentation for code you barely remember
All solved by: Well-organized projects

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Is a Project?

A self-contained folder containing everything needed to reproduce an analysis
Self-contained = All files in one folder
Everything needed = Data, scripts, outputs, documentation
Organized logically = Clear structure, logical names
For someone else = Collaborator, reviewer, future-you
Projects answer: 1. What data am I using? → data/ folder 2. What did I do? → documented in scripts 3. What did I produce? → saved in figures/

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Makes This Structure Good

✅ Clear hierarchy — Data, scripts, outputs separated
✅ Raw data protected — Never modified, in raw/ subfolder
✅ Scripts numbered — Know the order to run them
✅ Self-documenting — Folder and file names are descriptive
✅ Outputs separate — Nothing lost in script folders

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Raw vs. Processed Examples

Biology: - Raw: Field data with GPS errors, typos, missing dates - Processed: Corrected coordinates, standardized names, filled dates - Script: 01_clean_data.R creates processed from raw
Chemistry: - Raw: pH meter output with baseline drift, uncalibrated - Processed: Baseline-corrected, calibrated to standards - Script: 01_calibration.R creates processed from raw
Question for chat: Have you ever manually edited a dataset in Excel and saved over the original?
From now on: Raw data is read-only. All changes in code.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Absolute Paths (BAD)

This only works on MY computer:


# BAD - Absolute path
data <- read.csv("/Users/gretchen/Desktop/bee_analysis/data/raw/bees.csv")


Problem: You try to run this on your computer:
Error: cannot open file '/Users/gretchen/Desktop/...': 
No such file or directory
Why? You don’t have a user named “gretchen”

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Relative Paths (GOOD)

This works on ANYONE’s computer:


# GOOD - Relative path
data <- read.csv("data/raw/bees.csv")


Why it works:
“Starting from the project folder, go into data/, then raw/, and read bees.csv”
Works regardless of: - Your username - Where the project folder is located - Windows vs. Mac vs. Linux

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Relative Paths Matter

Scenario with absolute paths:

Finish analysis at school: C:/Users/Student/Documents/Research/data.csv

Work at home on laptop → ERROR (different path)
Manually fix all paths
Go back to school → ERROR (paths are wrong again)
Email advisor → ERROR (she doesn’t have your folders)

Scenario with relative paths:

Finish analysis at school: "data/raw/data.csv"

Work at home → Works

Go back to school → Works

Email advisor → Works


Relative paths make code portable

title: sfsu_data_sci

README Files: Bad Example

This is useless:

This is my analysis.


Tells you nothing: - What’s it about? - What data? - How to run it? - Who made it?

## Scripts (run in order)
1. `01_clean_data.R` - Removes incomplete surveys
2. `02_calculate_richness.R` - Rarefied richness
3. `03_make_figures.R` - Generates Figure 1

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git, GitHub, and the Scientific Audit Trail
Week 4, Day 2

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Welcome to Week 4, Day 2

Today: Git and GitHub as scientific tools
Not just for programmers!
Version control = audit trail for science

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Monday Recap

Monday: Why reproducibility fails

Ambiguity in workflows
Undocumented decisions
No audit trail of changes

Today: Git and GitHub solve these problems
Version control provides: - Complete history of changes - Who changed what, when, why - Ability to undo mistakes - Scientific accountability

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git vs. GitHub

Git = Version control software
Runs on your computer
Tracks changes to files
GitHub = Website/hosting service
Stores repositories online
Enables collaboration
Analogy:
Git = Word’s “Track Changes”
GitHub = Google Drive (but for code)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Scientists Need Version Control

Without Git: - analysis_v1.R, analysis_v2.R, analysis_final.R, analysis_FINAL_ACTUALLY.R - What changed between versions? - Why did you make that change? - Which version did you use for the paper?
With Git: - One file: analysis.R - Complete history of all changes - Commit messages explain why - Can tag specific versions

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Git Workflow

Artwork by Allison Horst

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Understanding the Workflow

Artwork by Allison Horst
The bunnies show us:
Local Repo (your computer) ← → Remote Repo (GitHub)
Push = Send your changes to GitHub
Pull = Get changes from GitHub
Bunnies in rowboats = Git doing the work!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Working Locally: Stage and Commit

Three areas:

Working Directory — where you edit files
Staging Area — files you’re about to commit
Local Repository — committed changes

Workflow: 1. Edit files 2. Stage changes you want to save (git add) 3. Commit with message (git commit -m "Fixed bug")

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Writing Good Commit Messages

Bad commit messages: - “fixed stuff” - “update” - “changes”
Good commit messages: - “Removed outliers < -50°C from temperature data” - “Added EPA water quality standards to comparison” - “Fixed bug in species name standardization”
Why? You’ll read these 6 months from now!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Syncing with GitHub: Push and Pull

After committing locally:
Push = Upload your commits to GitHub
git push
Before you start work:
Pull = Download changes from GitHub
git pull
Always pull before you push!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git Enables Scientific Collaboration

Artwork by Allison Horst

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
How Collaboration Works

Artwork by Allison Horst
Jenny Bryan (RStudio): “Git/GitHub is like agreeing that we will all use Microsoft Word…”
With Git: - Multiple people edit same project - Changes tracked individually - Can work simultaneously - Merge changes smoothly

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Collaborative Workflow

Owner: 1. Creates repository on GitHub 2. Adds collaborator 3. Pushes/pulls changes
Collaborator: 1. Clones repository 2. Makes changes locally 3. Commits changes 4. Pushes to GitHub
Both: - Pull frequently to get each other’s changes - Communicate about who’s working on what

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Merge Conflicts (And Why They’re OK)

What’s a merge conflict?
Two people edit the same line of code differently
Example: - You: Change temperature cutoff to -45°C - Partner: Change temperature cutoff to -55°C - Git doesn’t know which to keep!
Solution: 1. Git marks the conflict in the file 2. You decide which version to keep 3. Commit the resolved version
Conflicts = communication opportunity!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Two Ways to Use Git

Command Line Interface (CLI):
git status
git add analysis.R
git commit -m "Updated analysis"
git push
Graphical User Interface (GUI): - RStudio Git pane (click buttons!) - GitHub Desktop - GitKraken
Both do the same thing!
We’ll show you both approaches.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git in RStudio (GUI)

RStudio has built-in Git support!
Git pane shows: - Modified files (yellow M) - New files (green A) - Deleted files (red D)
Workflow: 1. Check boxes to stage files 2. Click Commit button 3. Write message 4. Click Push button
That’s it!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git on Command Line

Essential commands:
git status              # What changed?
git add filename.R      # Stage a file
git add .               # Stage all files
git commit -m "message" # Commit with message
git push                # Send to GitHub
git pull                # Get from GitHub
Why learn CLI? - More powerful - Works everywhere - Better for troubleshooting

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git Best Practices for Scientists

DO: ✅ Commit often (small, logical changes)
✅ Write clear commit messages
✅ Pull before you start work
✅ Push at end of work session
✅ Use .gitignore for large data files
DON’T: ❌ Commit huge changes all at once
❌ Use vague messages (“update”)
❌ Forget to pull before pushing
❌ Commit passwords or API keys
❌ Commit 100MB data files

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Using .gitignore

What is .gitignore?
File that tells Git what NOT to track
Common entries:
# Large data files
data/raw/big_dataset.csv

# Temporary files
*.tmp
*~

# System files
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# API keys
.env
secrets.R
Why? Keep repositories small and secure

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Tagging Important Versions

What are tags?
Named snapshots of your repository
Use tags for: - Paper submission: v1.0-submitted - Revisions: v1.1-revision1 - Final publication: v2.0-published - Presentations: esa-conference-2024
Why? Always know exactly what code produced published results
git tag v1.0-published
git push --tags

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git as Scientific Audit Trail

Git provides:
📝 Complete history — Every change documented
👤 Attribution — Who made each change
📅 Timestamps — When changes were made
💬 Rationale — Why (via commit messages)
🏷️ Milestones — Tags mark important versions
This is what reviewers and funders want to see!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
GitHub Beyond Storage

GitHub offers:
Issues — Track bugs, tasks, ideas
Projects — Organize work (like Trello)
README — Project documentation (already doing this!)
GitHub Pages — Host websites
Releases — Package specific versions
DOI integration — via Zenodo
Makes your science findable and citable!

text:
Key Concepts

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Reproducibility Fails (And How to Fix It)
Week 4, Day 1

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Welcome to Week 4!

This week: Reproducibility in practice
Monday: Why reproducibility fails
Wednesday: Git and GitHub (tools that help)
The uncomfortable truth: Most scientific analyses aren’t reproducible

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Where We’ve Been

Week 1: Data science thinking
Week 2: Projects and pseudocode (organization + planning)
Week 3: Quarto (combining code and narrative)
Today: The gap between theory and practice
Why reproducibility fails even when you try

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Reproducibility Matters

Artwork by Allison Horst

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reproducibility as Scientific Integrity

Artwork by Allison Horst
Without reproducibility: - Can’t verify results - Can’t build on prior work - Can’t trust conclusions
Reproducibility isn’t optional—it’s essential
It’s your scientific alibi

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Is Reproducibility?

Reproducibility = Someone else can take your data and code and get the same results
Not: - Replicability (collecting new data) - Just having data available - Describing methods in prose
Is: - Exact same results from same inputs - Including all intermediate steps - With clear documentation

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Reproducibility Crisis

Studies show: - 70% of researchers have tried and failed to reproduce another’s work - 50% have failed to reproduce their OWN work - Less than 30% of published studies share data AND code
In biology/ecology: - Many analyses impossible to reproduce - Methods sections insufficient - Code rarely shared

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Does Reproducibility Fail?

Not because scientists are careless!
Reproducibility fails due to: 1. Undocumented decisions 2. Fragile computational environments 3. Manual steps 4. Ambiguous workflows 5. Time pressure
Let’s examine each…

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reason 1: Undocumented Decisions

The problem:
You try outlier removal thresholds: 2 SD, 2.5 SD, 3 SD
You pick 2.5 SD (seems reasonable)
You don’t write this down
Six months later: Which threshold did you use?
Methods say: “Outliers were removed”
Reviewer asks: “How were outliers defined?”
You: ¯_(ツ)_/¯

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reason 2: Fragile Computational Environments

The problem:
Your analysis runs on: - R version 4.2.1 - ggplot2 version 3.4.0 - Your computer
Collaborator has: - R version 4.3.0 - ggplot2 version 3.4.2 - Different computer
Result: Different results or errors
Why? Package versions matter, OS matters

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reason 3: Manual Steps

The problem:
Your workflow: 1. Export data from instrument 2. Open in Excel, delete bad rows 3. Save as CSV 4. Run R script 5. Open plot, adjust colors in Photoshop 6. Insert in manuscript
Which rows deleted? What colors? Can’t reconstruct!
Solution: Everything in code

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Solution: Reproducible Workflows

Core principle:
Everything in code + version control

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Messy Desktop Problem

Desktop/
├── bee_data_final.csv
├── bee_data_final_FINAL.csv
├── bee_data_v3_USE_THIS_ONE.csv
├── analysis_draft.R
├── analysis_new.R
├── richness_plot.png
├── richness_plot_good.png
└── notes.txt


Questions you can’t answer: - Which data file is “real”? - Which script generated which plot? - How do you reproduce this?
Recognize this pattern?

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Cost of Disorganization

Scenario 1: Reviewer requests changes
→ Can’t figure out what you did 6 months ago
Scenario 2: Lab partner needs your code
→ Error: cannot open 'C:/Users/YourName/...'
Scenario 3: Journal requires code deposit
→ Week writing documentation for code you barely remember
All solved by: Well-organized projects

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Is a Project?

A self-contained folder containing everything needed to reproduce an analysis
Self-contained = All files in one folderEverything needed = Data, scripts, outputs, documentationOrganized logically = Clear structureFor someone else = Collaborator, reviewer, future-you
Projects answer: 1. What data? → data/ folder 2. What did I do? → documented in scripts 3. What did I produce? → saved in figures/

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
A Well-Organized Project

bee_diversity_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                # Original, untouched
│   └── processed/          # Cleaned data
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R     # Numbered = order
│   ├── 02_calculate_richness.R
│   └── 03_make_figures.R
├── figures/
├── README.md               # START HERE
└── bee_diversity.Rproj     # RStudio project


✅ Clear hierarchy | ✅ Protected raw data | ✅ Numbered scripts | ✅ Self-documenting

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Raw vs. Processed Data

data/
├── raw/         # What you started with
└── processed/   # What you created


Raw data = from field/lab/instrument
→ Never changes. Ever.
Processed data = created by cleaning raw data
→ Result of running a script
Golden rule:
Delete processed data and regenerate it by running scripts.
From now on: Raw data is read-only. All changes in code.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Paths Matter

Artwork by Allison Horst
The problem: Hardcoding file locations breaks everything

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Absolute vs. Relative Paths

Artwork by Allison Horst
The broken cube = setwd() and absolute paths (fragile!)The strong cube = R Projects (robust!)The skilled cube = here package (even better!)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Absolute Paths (BAD)

This only works on MY computer:


# BAD - Absolute path
data <- read.csv("/Users/gretchen/Desktop/bee_analysis/data/raw/bees.csv")


Error on your computer:
Error: cannot open file '/Users/gretchen/Desktop/...': 
No such file or directory
Why? You don’t have a user named “gretchen”

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Relative Paths (GOOD)

This works on ANYONE’s computer:


# GOOD - Relative path
data <- read.csv("data/raw/bees.csv")


Why it works:
“Starting from the project folder, go into data/, then raw/, read bees.csv”
Works on any computer, any operating system!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Relative Paths Save Your Life

With absolute paths:

Analysis at school: C:/Users/Student/.../data.csv

Work at home → ERROR (different path)
Fix all paths manually
Back at school → ERROR (wrong again)
Email advisor → ERROR (doesn’t have your folders)

With relative paths:

Analysis at school: "data/raw/data.csv"

Work at home → ✅ Works

Back at school → ✅ Works

Email advisor → ✅ Works

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Live Demo: Creating an RStudio Project

Follow along visually:
Step 1: Create project folder water_quality_analysis/
Step 2: Create subfolders:


water_quality_analysis/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
├── scripts/
└── figures/

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Creating the RStudio Project

Step 3: In RStudio:File > New Project > Existing Directory
Step 4: Create script scripts/01_load_data.R


# Load water quality data
water <- read.csv("data/raw/water_samples.csv")

# Check it loaded
head(water)


Notice: Path is "data/raw/..." not full path!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Testing Portability

Step 5: The test

Close RStudio
Move entire project folder to Desktop (or anywhere!)
Double-click .Rproj file
Run script again

Result: ✅ Still works!
Why? Relative paths are relative to project root

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Every Project Needs a README

README.md is the first thing anyone reads
Answers four questions: 1. What is this project about? 2. What data does it use? 3. How do I run the analysis? 4. Who do I contact?
Without README: Confusion and frustrationWith README: Clear path forward

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Bad README Example

# My Project

This is my analysis.


This tells you nothing: - What’s the research question? - What data? - How to run it? - Who made it?
Useless!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Good README Example

# Bee Diversity in Urban Gardens

## Overview
Analysis of bee species richness across 45 urban garden 
sites in San Francisco, May–August 2023.

Research question: Does richness differ between 
community gardens and private yards?

## Data
- Raw: `data/raw/bee_surveys.csv` (field surveys)
- Processed: `data/processed/bee_clean.csv` 

## Scripts (run in order)
1. `01_clean_data.R` - Removes incomplete surveys
2. `02_calculate_richness.R` - Rarefied richness
3. `03_make_figures.R` - Generates figures

## Contact
Gretchen LeBuhn (lebuhn@sfsu.edu)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Project Structure Checklist

Every project needs:
Folders: - [ ] data/raw/ — original, never modified - [ ] data/processed/ — cleaned/transformed - [ ] scripts/ — numbered if order matters - [ ] figures/ — all plots
Files: - [ ] .Rproj file - [ ] README.md - [ ] Descriptive file names

❌ No README
6 months later, no idea what anything does
❌ Too many versionsanalysis_final_REALLY_final_v3.R

Git, GitHub, and the Scientific Audit Trail
Week 4, Day 2

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Welcome to Week 4, Day 2

Today: Git and GitHub as scientific tools
Not just for programmers!
Version control = audit trail for science

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Monday Recap

Monday: Why reproducibility fails

Ambiguity in workflows
Undocumented decisions
No audit trail of changes

Today: Git and GitHub solve these problems
Version control provides: - Complete history of changes - Who changed what, when, why - Ability to undo mistakes - Scientific accountability

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git vs. GitHub

Git = Version control software
Runs on your computer
Tracks changes to files
GitHub = Website/hosting service
Stores repositories online
Enables collaboration
Analogy:
Git = Word’s “Track Changes”
GitHub = Google Drive (but for code)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Scientists Need Version Control

Without Git: - analysis_v1.R, analysis_v2.R, analysis_final.R, analysis_FINAL_ACTUALLY.R - What changed between versions? - Why did you make that change? - Which version did you use for the paper?
With Git: - One file: analysis.R - Complete history of all changes - Commit messages explain why - Can tag specific versions

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Git Workflow

Artwork by Allison Horst

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Understanding the Workflow

Artwork by Allison Horst
The bunnies show us:
Local Repo (your computer) ← → Remote Repo (GitHub)
Push = Send your changes to GitHub
Pull = Get changes from GitHub
Bunnies in rowboats = Git doing the work!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Working Locally: Stage and Commit

Three areas:

Working Directory — where you edit files
Staging Area — files you’re about to commit
Local Repository — committed changes

Workflow: 1. Edit files 2. Stage changes you want to save (git add) 3. Commit with message (git commit -m "Fixed bug")

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Writing Good Commit Messages

Bad commit messages: - “fixed stuff” - “update” - “changes”
Good commit messages: - “Removed outliers < -50°C from temperature data” - “Added EPA water quality standards to comparison” - “Fixed bug in species name standardization”
Why? You’ll read these 6 months from now!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Syncing with GitHub: Push and Pull

After committing locally:
Push = Upload your commits to GitHub
git push
Before you start work:
Pull = Download changes from GitHub
git pull
Always pull before you push!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git Enables Scientific Collaboration

Artwork by Allison Horst

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
How Collaboration Works

Artwork by Allison Horst
Jenny Bryan (RStudio): “Git/GitHub is like agreeing that we will all use Microsoft Word…”
With Git: - Multiple people edit same project - Changes tracked individually - Can work simultaneously - Merge changes smoothly

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Collaborative Workflow

Owner: 1. Creates repository on GitHub 2. Adds collaborator 3. Pushes/pulls changes
Collaborator: 1. Clones repository 2. Makes changes locally 3. Commits changes 4. Pushes to GitHub
Both: - Pull frequently to get each other’s changes - Communicate about who’s working on what

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Merge Conflicts (And Why They’re OK)

What’s a merge conflict?
Two people edit the same line of code differently
Example: - You: Change temperature cutoff to -45°C - Partner: Change temperature cutoff to -55°C - Git doesn’t know which to keep!
Solution: 1. Git marks the conflict in the file 2. You decide which version to keep 3. Commit the resolved version
Conflicts = communication opportunity!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Two Ways to Use Git

Command Line Interface (CLI):
git status
git add analysis.R
git commit -m "Updated analysis"
git push
Graphical User Interface (GUI): - RStudio Git pane (click buttons!) - GitHub Desktop - GitKraken
Both do the same thing!
We’ll show you both approaches.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git in RStudio (GUI)

RStudio has built-in Git support!
Git pane shows: - Modified files (yellow M) - New files (green A) - Deleted files (red D)
Workflow: 1. Check boxes to stage files 2. Click Commit button 3. Write message 4. Click Push button
That’s it!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git on Command Line

Essential commands:
git status              # What changed?
git add filename.R      # Stage a file
git add .               # Stage all files
git commit -m "message" # Commit with message
git push                # Send to GitHub
git pull                # Get from GitHub
Why learn CLI? - More powerful - Works everywhere - Better for troubleshooting

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git Best Practices for Scientists

DO: ✅ Commit often (small, logical changes)
✅ Write clear commit messages
✅ Pull before you start work
✅ Push at end of work session
✅ Use .gitignore for large data files
DON’T: ❌ Commit huge changes all at once
❌ Use vague messages (“update”)
❌ Forget to pull before pushing
❌ Commit passwords or API keys
❌ Commit 100MB data files

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Using .gitignore

What is .gitignore?
File that tells Git what NOT to track
Common entries:
# Large data files
data/raw/big_dataset.csv

# Temporary files
*.tmp
*~

# System files
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# API keys
.env
secrets.R
Why? Keep repositories small and secure

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Tagging Important Versions

What are tags?
Named snapshots of your repository
Use tags for: - Paper submission: v1.0-submitted - Revisions: v1.1-revision1 - Final publication: v2.0-published - Presentations: esa-conference-2024
Why? Always know exactly what code produced published results
git tag v1.0-published
git push --tags

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Git as Scientific Audit Trail

Git provides:
📝 Complete history — Every change documented
👤 Attribution — Who made each change
📅 Timestamps — When changes were made
💬 Rationale — Why (via commit messages)
🏷️ Milestones — Tags mark important versions
This is what reviewers and funders want to see!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
GitHub Beyond Storage

GitHub offers:
Issues — Track bugs, tasks, ideas
Projects — Organize work (like Trello)
README — Project documentation (already doing this!)
GitHub Pages — Host websites
Releases — Package specific versions
DOI integration — via Zenodo
Makes your science findable and citable!

Scenario: You and your lab partner both edited analysis.R
You changed line 45:

Key Concepts


Git = version control tracking all changes
GitHub = online hosting enabling collaboration
Push/Pull sync local and remote repositories

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:

title: sfsu_data_sci

Today: The gap between theory and practice

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Reproducibility Matters

Artwork by Allison Horst

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reproducibility as Scientific Integrity

Artwork by Allison Horst
Without reproducibility:
- Can’t verify results
- Can’t build on prior work
- Can’t trust conclusions
Reproducibility isn’t optional—it’s essential
It’s your scientific alibi

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Is Reproducibility?

Reproducibility = Someone else can take your data and code and get the same results
Not: - Replicability (collecting new data) - Just having data available - Describing methods in prose
Is: - Exact same results from same inputs - Including all intermediate steps - With clear documentation

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Reproducibility Crisis

Studies show:
- 70% of researchers have tried and failed to reproduce another’s work
- 50% have failed to reproduce their OWN work
- Less than 30% of published studies share data AND code
In biology/ecology:
- Many analyses impossible to reproduce
- Methods sections insufficient
- Code rarely shared

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Does Reproducibility Fail?

Not because scientists are careless!
Reproducibility fails due to:
1. Undocumented decisions
2. Fragile computational environments
3. Manual steps
4. Ambiguous workflows
5. Time pressure
Let’s examine each…

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reason 1: Undocumented Decisions

The problem:
You try outlier removal thresholds: 2 SD, 2.5 SD, 3 SD
You pick 2.5 SD (seems reasonable)
You don’t write this down
Six months later: Which threshold did you use?
Methods say: “Outliers were removed”
Reviewer asks: “How were outliers defined?”
You: ¯_(ツ)_/¯

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reason 2: Fragile Computational Environments

The problem:
Your analysis runs on: - R version 4.2.1 - ggplot2 version 3.4.0 - Your computer
Collaborator has: - R version 4.3.0 - ggplot2 version 3.4.2 - Different computer
Result: Different results or errors
Why? Package versions matter, OS matters

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reason 3: Manual Steps

The problem:
Your workflow: 1. Export data from instrument 2. Open in Excel, delete bad rows 3. Save as CSV 4. Run R script 5. Open plot, adjust colors in Photoshop 6. Insert in manuscript
Which rows deleted? What colors? Can’t reconstruct!
Solution: Everything in code

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
The Solution: Reproducible Workflows

Core principle:
Everything in code + version control
This solves:
- ✅ Undocumented decisions → Comments in code
- ✅ Fragile environments → Document packages
- ✅ Manual steps → Automate in code
- ✅ Ambiguous workflows → Clear structure
- ✅ Time pressure → Build habits now

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Reproducibility Checklist

Before sharing/publishing:

All steps in code (no manual steps)
Decisions documented in comments
File paths are relative
README explains how to run
Package versions documented
Code runs start-to-finish without errors
Someone else has successfully run it

If you can’t check all boxes, it’s not reproducible

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Pseudocode as Scientific Planning
Week 2, Day 2

BIO/CHEM 806

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Welcome!

Today: Pseudocode
Pseudocode = Writing down what you plan to do before you do it
Not intimidating! Just planning.

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Last Class Recap

Monday: Organizing projects
Folders, file structures, relative paths, READMEs
Today: How do you plan what goes inside those scripts?
Pseudocode bridges scientific thinking and code

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Pseudocode: Your Recipe

Artwork by Allison Horst

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Planning Before Cooking

Artwork by Allison Horst
Just like a chef plans their recipe before cooking:
Pseudocode = Your recipe (the plan)
Code = Cooking the meal (execution)
R/RStudio = Your kitchen and tools
Data = Your ingredients
You wouldn’t start cooking without a recipe!

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Is Pseudocode?

Step-by-step description of what you want your code to do, written in plain language

Not code
Not prose
Something in between

Think: Recipe for analysis
Clear enough someone could follow it
Specific enough = no ambiguity
General enough = not worrying about syntax

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Pseudocode Example

Bad (too vague): - “Clean the data”
Better (pseudocode): - “Load temperature data from CSV file” - “Remove rows where temperature is missing” - “Remove rows where temperature < -50 or > 60” - “Calculate mean temperature for each site” - “Save cleaned data to data/processed/temp_clean.csv”
See the difference?

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Why Pseudocode Matters

1. Forces you to think before you code
Most mistakes = typing before knowing what you’re doing
2. Reveals ambiguity
“Clean the data” seems clear… until you try to write pseudocode
3. Makes collaboration easier
Review logic before spending hours coding
Key insight: Good pseudocode translates to any programming language

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Pseudocode vs. Code vs. Prose

Prose (too informal): > “Remove bad data and make a graph”
Pseudocode (just right): - Load temperature data - Remove rows where temperature < -50 or > 60 - Create scatterplot of temperature vs. elevation - Save plot to figures/temp_elevation.png
Code (too specific):
data <- read.csv("data/raw/temps.csv")
data_clean <- data %>% filter(temperature >= -50, ...)

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
What Makes Good Pseudocode

Good pseudocode has:
✅ Verbs — Load, Remove, Calculate, Create, Save
✅ Specific conditions — “temperature < -50”, “absorbance > 3”
✅ Clear outputs — “scatterplot”, “save to figures/”
✅ Domain knowledge — “out of linear range”, “GPS error”
Detailed enough = unambiguous
General enough = not worrying about syntax

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Common Pseudocode Mistakes

Mistake 1: Too vague
❌ “Standardize the measurements”
✅ “Divide each mass by wing length to get body condition index”
Mistake 2: Too detailed (writing code)
❌ “Use filter() where count >= 5”
✅ “Remove sites with fewer than 5 observations”
Mistake 3: Skipping steps
❌ “Load data, make plot”
✅ “Load → Remove invalid → Calculate mean → Make bar plot”
Mistake 4: No decision points
❌ “Remove outliers”
✅ “Remove values more than 3 SD from mean”

title: sfsu_data_sci
text:
Pseudocode as Debugging Tool

Pseudocode isn’t just for planning—it’s for debugging!
When code fails, two possibilities:

Logic is flawed — asking computer to do wrong thing
Syntax is wrong — asking correctly but wrong words

With pseudocode: - Check: “Is this what I actually want to do?” - If pseudocode is right → syntax problem (easier!) - If pseudocode is wrong → fix logic first, then code
Saves hours of frustration

title: Week 1, Day 1: Data Science as Scientific Practice
text:
Duration: 75 minutes | Online Synchronous | 30 students




Test Zoom/conferencing platform
Prepare Google Doc template for breakout activity
Queue up welcome slide
Have chat window visible
Prepare breakout rooms (groups of 3-4, total 8-10 rooms)





[0:00–0:05] — Arrival and Settling
Good morning, everyone! Welcome to Biology/Chemistry 806. I’m Gretchen LeBuhn, and I’m co-teaching this course with Nicole Adelstein. We’re really glad you’re here.
Before we jump in, let’s take a moment to get settled. Grab water or tea if you need it, adjust your audio settings, and find a comfortable spot. We’re going to be together for 75 minutes, and I want you to feel present and ready to engage.
[Pause 3-4 seconds]
Quick tech check: If you can hear me clearly, give me a thumbs-up reaction or type “yes” in the chat.
Great! If your audio cuts out or something breaks during class, just pop a message in the chat and we’ll sort it out.




[0:05–0:10] — Setting the Tone
Before we dive into activities, I want to be clear about what this course is and what it isn’t.
This is a course about thinking clearly with data.
It’s not about being a coder already. It’s not about memorizing functions or learning statistics in isolation. It’s about learning to explain your reasoning, spot your own assumptions, and revise when something doesn’t make sense.
If you can do that kind of thinking in biology or chemistry, you can do it with data in R. If you struggle to do it in R, that’s not a coding problem — it’s a thinking problem, and we’ll work on it together.
[Pause]
Some of you might be wondering if you belong here. Maybe you’ve never written a line of code. Maybe you’ve used R a little and felt completely lost.
Let me be very clear: prior coding experience is not what matters here.
What matters is whether you’re willing to ask “why,” explain your choices, and revise when things are unclear. That’s science. We’re just applying it to data work.




[0:10–0:13] — Structure Preview
Here’s what we’re doing today:

Get to know each other — not in a forced icebreaker way, but in a way that helps us start noticing patterns in data
Use that process to surface big data science ideas — without touching code yet
Talk about norms — what you want from this class, what I want, and how we’ll work together

I’m not testing you today. I’m watching how you think, not what you already know.
Any questions before we start? You can unmute or use the chat.




[0:13–0:16] — Setting Up the Chat Activity
Okay, first activity. I want everyone to put three things in the chat:

Your name
Your field or program
One kind of data you work with — or hope to work with

If you’re not sure what counts as “data,” that’s totally fine. Just write what comes to mind. If you’ve never worked with data, write that. All answers are useful here.
You’ve got about two minutes. Go ahead and start typing!
[0:16–0:19] — Silent Typing Time
[Monitor chat. If people seem stuck after 30 seconds, you can add: “I’m seeing some great responses coming in. Remember, there’s no wrong answer here.”]

[0:19–0:26] — Reading and Commentary
Okay, I’m going to read some of these out loud — not to put anyone on the spot, but because I want us to start noticing patterns together.
[Read 6-8 responses, pausing to make observations]:

“Excel spreadsheets” — Notice that’s a format, not the phenomenon itself. Interesting distinction.
“Survey responses about student stress” — That’s behavioral data with a specific context.
“I’m not sure” — That’s an important answer too. Uncertainty is data about where we are in our learning.
“Gene sequences” — Molecular data with a very specific structure.

[Pause]
Let’s pause here. We just asked one simple question, and we got very different kinds of answers.
Here’s my question for you — and you can answer in the chat or unmute:
Did everyone interpret “data” the same way?

[0:26–0:30] — Processing Responses
[Read 3-4 chat responses aloud]
Yes. Exactly. Some people answered with the format (Excel, CSV). Some answered with the content (genes, behavior). Some answered with the collection method (surveys, sensors).
And here’s the thing: that ambiguity doesn’t go away when you start coding. It just gets buried under syntax.
In this class, we’re going to keep surfacing it. Because the hardest part of data science isn’t learning functions — it’s deciding what you’re even measuring and how to define it clearly.




[0:30–0:33] — Setting Up Breakout Activity
Okay, next activity. I’m going to put you into small groups of 3-4 people for about 10 minutes.
Here’s your task: Imagine you need to describe this class as a dataset for someone who wasn’t here today.

What variables would you include?
How would you define them?
What information do you wish you had?

I don’t want just a list of variable names. I want your reasoning. Why did you choose those variables? Where did you have to make judgment calls?
You’re going to work in a shared Google Doc — I’m dropping the template link in the chat right now.
[Drop link in chat]
Questions before I send you out?
[0:33–0:35] — Clarifications
[Answer 1-2 questions if needed]
Great. I’m sending you to breakout rooms now. Take the full 10 minutes — this is not a race.
I’ll pop into rooms briefly to check in. See you back here at [state exact time, e.g., 12:48].

[0:35–0:45] — BREAKOUT ROOMS
[Instructor visits 2-3 rooms briefly, listens, maybe asks one clarifying question]

[0:45–0:47] — Transition Back
Welcome back! I know 10 minutes goes fast when you’re actually thinking.
I’m going to ask three groups to share what they came up with — not everything, just one interesting decision you made or one place where you got stuck.
Can I have a volunteer from Group 3 to start us off? You can unmute or type in chat.




[0:47–0:58] — Report-Outs and Reframing
[Call on three groups. After each shares for ~2 minutes, you reframe]:
Example Group 1 shares about struggling to define “experience”:
I want to repeat that, because it’s important.
You wanted to measure “experience,” but you realized it’s not one thing. It could be time in a program, it could be prior statistics courses, it could be comfort with ambiguity, it could be years working with data.
And here’s what matters: You didn’t fail because you couldn’t agree. You succeeded because you noticed the decision you’d have to make — and that decision has consequences.
If you measure experience as “years in grad school,” you’ll get a different analysis than if you measure it as “number of R courses taken.” Both are defensible. Neither is invisible.
That’s data science.
[Repeat this pattern for 2 more groups, ~3-4 minutes each]

[0:58–1:02] — Explicit Connection
Okay, let’s step back. What did we just do?
Without writing a single line of code, you: - Defined variables - Noticed ambiguity - Made decisions and justified them - Realized that someone else might make different decisions — and that’s okay
That’s the foundation of everything we’ll do this semester.
On Wednesday, we’ll start putting those decisions into words more formally using something called a “decision log.” But today, I wanted you to feel what it’s like to think carefully about data before you touch a computer.




[1:02–1:05] — Transition
We’ve got about 13 minutes left, and I want to spend them talking about how we’ll work together this semester.
I’m going to share a few norms I think are important. Then I want to hear from you — what do you need from this class? What do you want to accomplish?

[1:05–1:10] — Your Commitments
Here’s what I’m committing to:

I will not assume you know things. If I use a term you haven’t seen, stop me.
I will not mistake speed for understanding. Going slow is not a problem. Going fast without learning is.
I will not treat “I don’t know” as failure. It’s the start of figuring something out.
I will give you time to think before you answer. Silence is not dead air — it’s thinking space.

And here’s what I need from you:

Ask questions out loud, not just in your head. If you’re confused, someone else is too.
Try things even when you’re not sure. I’d rather see your messy reasoning than a polished guess.
Be kind to each other and to yourselves. This course is hard because thinking clearly is hard, not because I’m trying to trick you.


[1:10–1:12] — Opening It Up
Okay, your turn. I’m going to ask two questions. You can answer in the chat or unmute:

What do you want to accomplish this semester?
What do you need from me or from each other to make that happen?

Take a moment to think. Then start sharing.
[Give 5-7 seconds of silence]

[1:12–1:18] — Student Voices
[Read responses, acknowledge them briefly]:
“I want to feel competent, not just compliant.” — Yes. That’s exactly what we’re here for.
“I want to understand what I’m doing, not just copy code.” — Absolutely. Understanding is the goal.
“I need patience when I’m stuck.” — You’ll have it. From me and from each other.

[1:18–1:20] — Synthesis
I’m hearing a few themes: - You want to feel competent, not just compliant - You want to understand, not just copy - You want space to struggle without judgment
I can work with that. We all can. Let’s hold each other to these commitments.




[1:20–1:22] — Preview and Closing
Before Wednesday, I want you to think about this question:
What decisions did we make today that felt invisible at the time?
We’re not writing code yet, but we’re already making choices about what counts, what matters, and how to define things.
On Wednesday, we’ll practice writing those choices down clearly using something called a decision log. It’s going to feel weird at first. That’s okay.

[1:22–1:25] — Final Thoughts
One last thing before we go.
Everything we did today — the thinking, the struggling with definitions, the noticing ambiguity — that’s not “pre-data-science.”
That IS data science.
The coding is just execution. The thinking is the work.
See you Wednesday. Thanks for being here and for engaging so thoughtfully.
[Stay online for 2-3 minutes for questions]

Google Doc template: “Describe this class as a dataset. What variables would you include? How would you define them? What information do you wish you had?”
Slides (see accompanying slide deck)
Chat enabled
Reactions enabled (thumbs up, etc.)






Pacing: Build in pauses. Online students need processing time.
Engagement: Call on specific groups/people by name when possible
Backup plan: If breakout rooms fail, use collaborative Google Doc with sections for each “group”
Accessibility: Keep chat open for those who prefer not to unmute
